articles.title: Weniger Homeoffice: Warum Arbeitgeber die Flexibilität ihrer Teams laut Umfrage weiter reduzieren
articles.text:
Homeoffice auf dem Rückzug: Nur noch 54 Prozent der Unternehmen erlauben mobiles Arbeiten
Wer in Deutschland einen Job im Homeoffice sucht, wird immer öfter enttäuscht. Laut einer repräsentativen Bitkom-Umfrage erlauben nur noch 54 Prozent der mehr als 600 befragten Unternehmen ihren Mitarbeiter:innen, zumindest gelegentlich von zuhause zu arbeiten. Gleichzeitig geben mehr als drei Viertel an, Menschen zu beschäftigen, deren Tätigkeiten sich grundsätzlich auch außerhalb eines festen Büros erledigen ließen. Seit dem Ende der Pandemie ist der Homeoffice-Trend messbar rückläufig.
Homeoffice-Tage werden weiter gekürzt
Wiederholte Lockdowns und Kontaktbeschränkungen zwangen seit dem Ausbruch des Coronavirus im Frühjahr 2020 einen Großteil der Unternehmen, ihre Teams ins Homeoffice zu schicken. Dabei zeigte sich schnell, dass Angestellte auch ohne Präsenzpflicht gute Ergebnisse erzielen. Trotzdem begannen viele Unternehmen, die Homeoffice-Tage nach und nach zu reduzieren. Laut Bitkom trifft das auf mehr als die Hälfte der Unternehmen zu: 39 Prozent haben die Option seit dem Ende der Pandemie reduziert und 17 Prozent haben sie sogar ganz abgeschafft. Nur bei 29 Prozent der befragten Unternehmen sind die Regelungen unverändert geblieben.
Wie häufig Beschäftigte mobil oder im Homeoffice arbeiten dürfen, hängt stark von der Unternehmensgröße ab. Größere Unternehmen setzen häufiger auf flexible Regelungen ohne feste Zahl an Homeoffice-Tagen. Bei Unternehmen mit 20 bis 99 Beschäftigten sind es 28 Prozent, bei 100 bis 499 Beschäftigten 34 Prozent und bei mehr als 500 Beschäftigten 41 Prozent. Dort entscheiden die Beschäftigten selbst, an wie vielen Tagen sie mobil arbeiten möchten. Insgesamt bieten 29 Prozent der Unternehmen, die mobiles Arbeiten ermöglichen, dieses maximal flexible Modell an. 17 Prozent erlauben mehrere Homeoffice-Tage pro Woche und 20 Prozent immerhin einen Tag. Nur bei drei Prozent ist Homeoffice seltener als einmal pro Woche möglich.
Viele sehen im Homeoffice klare Vorteile
Laut Bitkom-Hauptgeschäftsführer Bernhard Rohleder überrascht es kaum, dass Unternehmen die Möglichkeit wieder reduzieren. Während der Pandemie war Homeoffice Pflicht. Jetzt können Arbeitgeber:innen wieder selbst entscheiden, wann und wo ihre Teams arbeiten sollen. 35 Prozent der befragten Unternehmen wollen die Homeoffice-Möglichkeiten weiter reduzieren, ein kleiner Teil von drei Prozent plant sogar, bestehende Regelungen komplett abzuschaffen. Dafür nennen sie mehrere Gründe: 65 Prozent sagen, durch Homeoffice gehe der Zusammenhalt im Unternehmen verloren. Weitere 60 Prozent meinen, Homeoffice erschwere die Integration neuer Beschäftigter.
Dennoch sehen die Unternehmen in Deutschland, die ihren Angestellten zumindest gelegentlich das Arbeiten von zuhause oder anderswo erlauben, oft klare Vorteile. 71 Prozent sagen, ihre Teams könnten durch die Flexibilität Familie und Beruf besser miteinander vereinbaren. Mehr als sechs von zehn Unternehmen sind zudem der Meinung, dass es ohne Homeoffice-Option schwieriger sei, gute Mitarbeiter:innen zu finden. 39 Prozent vertreten sogar die Auffassung, im Homeoffice seien ihre Teams in der Regel produktiver als im Büro. Einige ziehen daraus praktische Konsequenzen: Laut Bitkom haben 14 Prozent der befragten Unternehmen ihre Homeoffice-Möglichkeiten seit der Hochphase der Pandemie ausgeweitet oder neu eingeführt. Aber nur drei Prozent der Unternehmen planen eine Ausweitung.

articles.title: À bord de sa station spatiale Tiangong, la Chine frôle le zéro absolu et bat un record du monde
articles.text:
Le zéro absolu, à −273,15 °C, est la température à laquelle les atomes seraient parfaitement immobiles. On ne peut jamais l’atteindre, mais une équipe chinoise vient de s’en approcher comme personne avant elle : à bord de la station spatiale Tiangong, elle a refroidi un nuage d’atomes de rubidium à 9,7 picokelvins, soit 9,7 billionièmes de degré au-dessus du zéro absolu (le zéro absolu correspondant à 0 Kelvin).
Ces travaux, menés par l’université de Pékin et l’Institut d’optique et de mécanique fine de Shanghai, sont parus ce jeudi 5 novembre 2026 dans la revue Science. L’étude elle-même n’est pas accessible gratuitement, mais Science donne plus de détails dans un autre article. Le précédent record, 38 picokelvins, était tenu depuis 2021 par une équipe allemande, rappelle l’agence officielle chinoise Xinhua.
Pourquoi aller dans l’espace pour battre ce record ?
Que veut dire une température aussi basse ? Elle mesure l’agitation des atomes : à ce niveau, ils avancent à moins de 200 micromètres par seconde, soit un cinquième de millimètre. Or, au sol, la gravité les plaque contre le champ qui les retient, ce qui les réchauffe. En apesanteur, un piège laser beaucoup plus faible suffit, et les atomes restent observables 7 secondes. Soit bien plus que la durée de 2 secondes observée lors d’une expérience dans une tour d’impesanteur sur Terre, ou la durée de 1 seconde observée à bord de l’ISS.
Pour réussir cet exploit, les chercheurs ont piégé des atomes de rubidium dans des faisceaux laser, évacué les plus chauds en baissant la puissance lumineuse, puis laissé les survivants se détendre dans un piège élargi pour faire chuter leurs interactions à un niveau record.
Holger Mueller, physicien à l’université de Californie à Berkeley, estime d’ailleurs dans Science que « ces 7 secondes constituent un critère de performance encore plus important que les 10 picokelvins » (en arrondissant le résultat présenté par les scientifiques). Il ajoute : « Un jour, quelqu’un parviendra peut-être à obtenir sur Terre une température aussi basse que 10 picokelvins, mais il ne pourra pas la maintenir en chute libre pendant 7 secondes. »
Le chiffre est accompagné d’une marge d’erreur, qui va de 7 à 12,9 picokelvins d’après Phys.org. L’Académie chinoise des sciences invite déjà les chercheurs du monde entier à se servir de l’instrument.

articles.title: How we review 4x more AI code without reading every line
articles.text:
How we review 4x more AI code without reading every line
Do you need to read every line of AI-generated code to trust it?
Not necessarily. Instead, check five things: the intent behind a change, its acceptance criteria, the invariants it can’t break, the decisions made along the way, and evidence that it works.
At Aviator, that shift let the same nine engineers merge 4× more pull requests, cut median time to merge from 2.1 days to 3.4 hours, and drop reverts by 40%. A human still signs off on every PR. What changed is what that human reads.
“Decisions need a person, and a diff is the worst place to make them.”
We got the insight by sorting our own review comments. Most of what a reviewer writes on a PR is either a rule they’ve written before or a decision. Machines should check rules every time. Decisions need a person, and a diff is the worst place to make them.
The problem: Code review doesn’t scale with AI
Our code flipped from human-written with AI help to AI-generated with human help. Weekly merged PRs went from about 100 to more than 400. Our median AI-generated PR reached 640 lines, well past 400 lines, widely considered the limit where bug detection falls off.
Catching bugs was never the main point of code review anyway. In Microsoft’s 2013 study (Bacchelli & Bird), only 14% of review comments were about defects. Review is how engineers share knowledge and keep their mental model of the system current, and that’s the part worth protecting. When agents write most of the code, it’s also the part most at risk.
“Catching bugs was never the main point of code review anyway. Review is how engineers share knowledge and keep their mental model of the system current, and that’s the part worth protecting.”
Since I argued that code reviews are dead, the most common pushback I hear is, “So you just stopped reviewing?” No. We stopped reviewing the diff.
So, what didn’t work?
- An AI reviewer. On one of my own PRs, it opened 16 of 18 threads: magic numbers, array-index React keys, a component that ran too long. One thread caught a real race condition. The two comments that mattered, both design decisions from teammates, got buried under nits.
- A four-hour review SLA. We couldn’t add reviewers, so we added a rule. First reviews got faster, and approvals got emptier, as reviewers skimmed to hit the clock and their own work stalled.
- A self-review skill tuned to our conventions. Its findings were far better than the generic bot’s. But it still read the diff after the code was written, and the most useful part of the exchange, what it argued about and what we decided, died in a chat window.
All three tried to read the diff better. But the diff is the least important part of code review anyway. It shows what changed, never why.
To see what review actually contained, I went back to a PR I’d reviewed in 2025. It had 14 threads. Eight came from a bot and caught one real bug. Three of my six comments were rules I’d already written on other PRs, like “Use GraphQLRetryableException so Celery retries on it.” Only two were real decisions, like “No comments extracted: should we tell the user on the PR?”
What did work: Verify intent, not lines
Code review used to do several jobs at once: catch bugs, enforce team conventions, settle design decisions, and keep everyone’s understanding of the system current. We split those jobs up and gave each one a better home.
Argue before the PR exists. Our review agent cross-examines the author’s agent, running on a different model, and writes down every disagreement. On one recent PR, the agents raised four disagreements and settled three with a stated reason. The only one left for a human was a naming call.
Capture intent and acceptance criteria. Not as an up-front spec, but captured from the coding session with the agent. Every time an engineer corrects the agent or answers its question, we create a criterion. We used to throw those away when the session ended. Intent answers why we’re making the change; acceptance criteria answer how it should behave. Intent without criteria can’t be checked, and criteria without intent can’t be judged.
“Intent answers why we’re making the change; acceptance criteria answer how it should behave. Intent without criteria can’t be checked, and criteria without intent can’t be judged.”
Codify repeated comments as invariants. We mined a year of review history in three passes: drop the noise (bot summaries, bare “LGTMs”), classify every comment as a rule, proposal, one-off fix, or question, then merge the repeats. 11,400 comments became 212 candidate rules and 64 approved invariants. Each has a scope, a verification method, provenance, and an owner.
Take “Every config change writes an audit-log entry, only when something changed.” It covers GraphQL mutations and API handlers that write config, is verified by a preview run that saves twice and reads the audit log, was mined from 23 review threads across 17 PRs, and belongs to the platform team.
A model checking every invariant on every PR is slow and not perfectly repeatable, so where possible an agent compiles invariants into ast-grep rules that run in shadow beside the model until they agree. A comment we’d left on nine PRs, “Add a timeout, this hung a worker,” is now an eight-line rule. Nineteen invariants run deterministically, in 0.3 seconds.
Prove every criterion with evidence. Each criterion becomes a scenario. An agent spins up a preview environment, drives it like a user, and records screenshots, requests, and logs. For the audit-log invariant, it saves a setting, confirms one new log entry, saves again with nothing changed, and confirms there’s still one.
That second half is exactly what a reviewer reading the diff would never check. Not every criterion needs a browser: an API contract is proven by a recorded request and response, a code rule by an ast-grep match or a file-and-line citation. Pick the cheapest proof that settles the question. A green CI check only says the tests you thought of passed.
Debate the decisions. Decisions come from three places: the coding session, the agents’ argument, and failed verification runs. The PR lists every one, where it came from, and who settled it. On a PR that added retries for failed webhook deliveries, four of five decisions were settled; the agents disagreed on whether to deduplicate retried deliveries, so a person settled that one.
Reviewers skim what’s settled, settle what the agents couldn’t, reopen anything they’d call differently, and talk it through with the author. That conversation builds understanding of the system.
Own the rules. Engineers stop reading every line. They own the rules that check every line, and keep their understanding of the system by reading intent, evidence, and decisions.
The results
- PRs merged per week: 4×, with the same nine engineers
- Median time to merge: 2.1 days → 3.4 hours
- Human threads per PR: 6.2 → 1.3
- Reverts per 100 PRs: down 40%
Review work didn’t disappear. It moved to refining invariants, debating decisions, and improving verification. Expect the transition to hurt: month one is double work, by month two invariants catch up enough that reviews shrink, and by month three you read intent and evidence, not code.

articles.title: Un grupo de residentes de Pleasanton busca restricciones más fuertes en la privacidad de datos para una flota de robots
articles.text:
Los vecinos de Pleasanton, California, llevan varias semanas compartiendo sus calles con unos pequeños robots. Todo forma parte de un proyecto municipal destinado a detectar problemas de accesibilidad, pero el problema es que no todos los residentes están convencidos de que su actividad se limite a examinar el pavimento.
Algunos han comenzado a cuestionar qué información recopilan estas máquinas y qué ocurre con esos datos una vez que terminan su recorrido. Según explica Pleasanton Weekly, la preocupación surgió después de que Brent Werder (ingeniero especializado en robótica) observara cómo uno de estos dispositivos permanecía durante unas 7 horas frente a su vivienda.
Así, el vecino aseguró que vio robots girando sus cámaras hacia peatones, vehículos e incluso ventanas, y justo por eso revisó el contrato municipal. Tras comprobar que no establecía suficientes restricciones sobre el tratamiento de los datos, decidió impulsar una petición ciudadana para exigir mayores garantías.
La empresa asegura que sus robots no recopilan información personal
Los dispositivos desarrollados por Daxbot trabajan en colaboración con Bureau Veritas dentro de un programa que contempla examinar 580 kilómetros de aceras y caminos. Así, la intención del Ayuntamiento es identificar obstáculos y otros problemas que dificulten los desplazamientos de personas con movilidad reducida.
Sin embargo, Werder considera que el contrato debería especificar qué información se almacena, el tiempo y quién tendrá acceso a ella, así como exigir la eliminación de los datos que no resulten necesarios. Desde Daxbot rechazan que sus máquinas estén realizando labores de vigilancia encubierta, y Miriam Sullivan, responsable de comunicación de la compañía, asegura que los robots no identifican ni siguen a personas ni almacenan vídeos, salvo cuando se produce algún incidente de seguridad.
El Ayuntamiento de Pleasanton, por su parte, respalda esta explicación y sostiene que solo se recoge información relacionada con las infraestructuras peatonales. Pese a ello, los vecinos que impulsan la petición quieren que esas garantías queden reflejadas expresamente en las condiciones del proyecto.

articles.title: The NASA Artemis II launch punched two 5,000 km holes in the ionosphere that disrupted GPS signals, study finds
articles.text:
Ripple effect: Earlier this year, the Artemis II mission carried astronauts around the Moon and back for the first time in more than half a century. According to researchers, the historic mission also took a "heavy" toll on our planet's outermost ionized atmospheric layer.
This April's Artemis II mission caused two large holes in Earth's ionosphere, resulting in significant disturbances that could affect GPS positioning accuracy. A new study by Taiwan-based researchers highlighted how modern launch systems can impact the atmosphere, and how future exploration missions are going to affect one of the most important orbiting systems in everyday life.
The study was published in the pre-print online edition of the Geophysical Research Letters journal by a team of scientists working at Taiwan's National Cheng Kung University. The researchers used a network of ground-based, high-precision GPS receivers to detect the impact of the Artemis II launch. The same network is currently used by US scientists to measure tiny movements in Earth's tectonic plates during earthquakes.
The ground-based network can detect how free electrons in the ionosphere are affected by a rocket piercing through the atmosphere, measuring the delay in GPS signals traveling from orbiting satellites to the receiving network. The ionosphere is the ionized part of Earth's upper atmosphere, ranging from 48 km to 965 km (around 30 to 600 miles) above sea level.
The ionosphere plays a crucial role in the propagation of radio signals traveling around the globe, and any disruption to its electromagnetic field can also affect GPS signals. According to the new study, the initial Artemis II launch was more powerful than any other rocket launch to date. NASA's Space Launch System (SLS) caused a disturbance in the ionosphere that was ten times more severe than the ones observed during SpaceX's Starship tests.
The researchers said that Artemis II caused two big electromagnetic holes in Earth's ionosphere. The first event was caused by the 65-meter-long (213 foot) core stage of the SLS launcher, while the other one was left behind by two subsequent thruster burns of the system's upper stage. Both these holes spanned 5,000 km (around 3,107 miles) and were enough to cause the GPS system to miss the reported ground position by several meters.
According to professor Charles Lin, one of the co-authors of the new study, the disrupted GPS signal "could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning."
"A positioning error of a couple of meters is enough to cause an autonomous car to change lanes," Lin said.
The GPS satellite constellation orbits the planet at around 20,200 km (12,552 miles) above sea level, far above the ionosphere. However, GPS signals have to travel through all the layers of the lower atmosphere before reaching users' smartphones, ground stations, and self-driving cars. Lin now expects that future missions, including those going to the Moon's surface and Mars, will likely increase the potential disruption of the GPS service.

articles.title: TSMC denies exploring 3D DRAM at Nvidia's request — advanced memory tech is still years from market viability
articles.text:
TSMC denies exploring 3D DRAM at Nvidia's request — advanced memory tech is still years from market viability
Does TSMC need DRAM to capitalize on DRAM?
A recent report from The Information suggested that TSMC is exploring 3D DRAM production at Nvidia's request as surging demand for AI hardware strains global DRAM supplies and drives up prices. If the proposal were to come to fruition, it could mean a new, albeit prone to cyclical risks, business for TSMC and could dramatically expand its role in the AI supply chain. For its part, TSMC states that it is a pure-play logic foundry and plans to remain a logic foundry, which essentially means a denial of the report.
"Please note that TSMC focuses on our core business at all times, which is dedicated IC foundry," a TSMC spokesperson told Tom's Hardware. "Our mission is to be the trusted technology and capacity provider of the global logic IC industry for years to come."
Despite the denial, according to two people familiar with the initiative cited by The Information, TSMC has begun preparing plans for 3D DRAM manufacturing following a request from Nvidia, its largest customer. The initiative is reportedly overseen by Hsu Kuo-chin, TSMC’s vice president responsible for advanced packaging and former head of Micron’s Taiwanese operations. The effort comes amid widespread memory shortages that turned memory from a commodity into a strategic asset that could determine whether a company can ship its products to customers or not.
Although TSMC works closely with DRAM producers as it packages memory into system-in-packages (SiPs) for its customers, the company lacks the expertise and production capacity to make DRAM, let alone 3D DRAM. Meanwhile, given that 3D DRAM is years away even for major memory makers, pursuing a 3D DRAM strategy cannot solve memory shortages for at least five years.
Unlike conventional DRAM, which arranges memory cells in a single plane, 3D DRAM places multiple levels of memory cells vertically to increase capacity per wafer. All three leading DRAM makers — Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix — are working on their 3D DRAM projects. However, Micron's DRAM strategy includes at least four more planar DRAM process technologies before 3D DRAM becomes a reality.
While TSMC has arguably the industry's best logic process technologies, DRAM production requires entirely different manufacturing processes, which TSMC would have to develop, should it pursue making memory for its customers. Meanwhile, producing 3D DRAM requires completely different fabrication techniques to construct multiple memory-cell layers while controlling defects and maintaining acceptable yields. It is hardly possible to develop a 3D DRAM manufacturing process without having a competitive planar DRAM process technology, and TSMC does not have one.
One of the options for TSMC to enter the DRAM business would be to acquire a small specialty memory producer that has its own fabrication capability. This would give TSMC a credible route into advanced DRAM manufacturing without having to develop the underlying memory technology and IPs from scratch. However, small makers do not have leading-edge commodity DRAM nodes, so TSMC would still need to invest billions of dollars and years of R&D into development of a leading-edge process technology for DRAM.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
However, entering DRAM manufacturing would expose TSMC to substantial market risks. Memory shortages frequently encourage capacity expansions that eventually create oversupply, depressing prices and profitability. Such uncertainty could surely make TSMC think twice before going down the DRAM route. Furthermore, entering the DRAM business could also complicate TSMC's relationship with large DRAM makers in general, and SK Hynix, which partnered with the foundry in 2024 to manufacture logic base dies for next-generation HBM products, in particular.
TSMC’s potential entry into DRAM manufacturing could also raise antitrust questions, particularly if the company combines its dominant position in leading-edge logic manufacturing, leading position in advanced chip packaging, and ramping memory production. Regulators could examine whether such vertical integration would enable TSMC to favor its own memory products or disadvantage competitors that lack such a vertical integration. Then again, in-house DRAM development by TSMC could also strengthen competition by introducing another supplier into a market dominated by just three manufacturers.
Yet, TSMC does not necessarily need to manufacture DRAM to capitalize on growing demand for advanced memory. Instead, it could capture a larger share of the value generated by DRAM by producing sophisticated logic base dies for HBM, integrating memory with processors using its SoIC hybrid bonding technology, and developing customized memory solutions with partners such as GUC and established DRAM manufacturers. This approach would allow TSMC to expand its presence in the advanced memory market without investing billions of dollars in developing competitive DRAM process technologies from scratch and/or building additional fabs for tens of billions of dollars.

Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: De MacBook a bolsa para empreender: o ‘pacote dos sonhos’ de demissão da Canva
articles.text:
Seis meses de salário, assistência médica por um ano, MacBook da empresa e auxílio para empreender. Esses são os destaques do pacote de demissão da Canva.
A plataforma australiana de design anunciou, na terça-feira (03), uma reestruturação que vai afetar 1.271 funcionários – 22% dos seus colaboradores.
Entre as mudanças, estão demissões, alterações de funções e pedidos de transferência para outras cidades.
O ‘pacote dos sonhos’ de demissão da Canva
Para começar, o pacote de demissão da Canva prevê pelo menos seis meses de salário, independentemente do país onde o funcionário trabalhou. O valor inclui os direitos trabalhistas previstos na legislação de cada país.
Além disso, o pacote prevê que o Canva Care, programa de assistência médica a funcionários e familiares, será mantido por um ano.
O pacote inclui orientação para carreira, preparação para entrevistas e até assinatura por um ano do LinkedIn Premium.
A Canva também diz que vai criar um cadastro de ex-funcionários e compartilhá-lo com investidores, parceiros e contatos do setor.
O pacote também permite que os funcionários demitidos fiquem com o MacBook que a empresa disponibilizava para eles trabalharem.
A companhia também anunciou a criação do Canva Collective Fund. Este fundo vai conceder bolsas de US$ 10 mil (R$ 54,8 mil) a funcionários demitidos que queiram desenvolver algum projeto.
A bolsa poderá ser usada para abrir um negócio ou desenvolver iniciativas voltadas para a comunidade local.
A Canva informou que não exigirá participação nos negócios nem terá direitos sobre os projetos desenvolvidos graças ao fundo.
Pedro Spadoni é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de Piracicaba. Já escreveu para sites, revistas e jornal.

articles.title: ¿Tu PC se está quedando sin espacio? Esta carpeta de Windows podría tener parte de culpa
articles.text:
Windows 11 cumplió cinco años el pasado 5 de octubre. Y aunque no tuvo una bienvenida demasiado calurosa por culpa de sus exigentes requisitos mínimos, a base de actualizaciones y otras estrategias, Microsoft ha logrado que esta versión de Windows esté presente en el 71,5% de los ordenadores de escritorio. Curiosamente, cinco años después de su lanzamiento, Windows 11 sigue sorprendiéndonos con su forma de trabajar. Por ejemplo. ¿Sabías que Windows guarda los instaladores, parches y actualizaciones en una carpeta oculta llamada Windows Installer? ¿Y que si la dejamos crecer puede llegar a ocupar más de 10 GB?
El espacio disponible en el disco duro del ordenador es siempre un tema de discusión. Y más hoy en día, con el precio que están alcanzando procesadores, tarjetas gráficas, memorias y discos SSD y HDD. A medida que van pasando los meses, a base de instalar y actualizar aplicaciones y juegos, tus discos van menguando. Y, en ocasiones, es el propio Windows el que provoca esta situación, como vimos este verano. La buena noticia es que siempre hay maneras de ganar algo de espacio.
Hoy vamos a centrarnos en un causante de esta falta de espacio en disco, la carpeta Windows Installer. O simplemente, Installer. En realidad, es un componente importante de Windows. Pero su funcionamiento hace que, con el tiempo, se convierta en un problema más que en una solución. Veamos para qué sirve exactamente y cómo puedes limpiarla sin ocasionar un estropicio en tu ordenador.
Para qué sirve la carpeta Windows Installer
Es habitual encontrar en foros de internet comentarios sobre la carpeta Installer o Windows Installer. Su ruta es C:\Windows\Installer. No intentes buscarla en el Explorador de Windows, no la encontrarás porque está oculta. Por motivos de seguridad. Sin embargo, sí la verás si analizas el espacio disponible con herramientas como el Liberador de espacio en disco de Windows.
Esta carpeta es la caché de Windows Installer, es decir, una carpeta oculta que guarda copias de los paquetes MSI y parches MSP que utiliza Windows para instalar aplicaciones, repararlas, actualizarlas y, llegado el momento, desinstalarlas. Su razón de ser es que, cuando tengas un problema con las apps ya instaladas, no tengas que volver a descargar su instalador. Ya lo tendrás ahí listo para hacer su función.
Esta memoria caché de Windows Installer es importante para el buen funcionamiento de Windows y de las aplicaciones. En concreto, para desinstalar y actualizar aplicaciones. Según la documentación oficial de Microsoft, “los archivos que faltan no se pueden copiar entre equipos porque los archivos son únicos”. Y, a continuación, detalla una serie de códigos y mensajes de error que te puedes encontrar si faltan esos archivos. Básicamente, si tienes que reparar o actualizar una aplicación. Llegado el caso, probablemente tendrás que reinstalarla. Y esto puede ser un verdadero problema con aplicaciones como Microsoft Office, Visual Studio o cualquier herramienta de Adobe, por citar los ejemplos más mencionados.
Por qué no hay que tocar esa carpeta
La lógica nos dice que si algo ocupa mucho espacio, la solución más sencilla es borrar. No ya la carpeta, pero sí los archivos que contiene. Sin embargo, la documentación oficial desaconseja que borres o vacíes la carpeta Windows Installer manualmente. A ver, no vas a romper Windows. Pero puede que el problema te lo encuentres en cuanto abras una aplicación al azar.
Hay que tener en cuenta que no todos los archivos son susceptibles de ser borrados. Especialmente si están almacenados dentro de la carpeta Windows. Es la carpeta reservada al sistema operativo, así que siempre hay que ir con cautela con esa carpeta. Tocar algo de ahí puede ocasionar problemas del sistema. Que tal vez no notes al instante, pero sí que los verás al cabo de unos días. Y tal vez en el momento más inoportuno.
Esto no implica que debas resignarte y conformarte con que la carpeta Windows Installer engorde sin fin. Hay varias soluciones a las que puedes acudir para ganar más espacio y limpiar correctamente la caché de Windows Installer. Veamos las más efectivas. En realidad, son las que todo el mundo suele recomendar cuando tienes que limpiar Windows para que funcione mejor o tenga más espacio disponible.
Limpiar la carpeta Installer de forma segura
Para limpiar la carpeta Windows Installer tan solo necesitas las herramientas que ya ofrece Windows por defecto. Existen soluciones externas, pero no son necesarias. Para empezar, abre la aplicación Liberador de espacio en disco. Puedes hacerlo desde el buscador del menú Inicio de Windows. Y aunque no hace milagros, siempre te ayudará a liberar algo de espacio en disco.
En esta ocasión, además de la lista de Archivos que se pueden eliminar, para incluir la carpeta Windows Installer tendrás que hacer clic en Limpiar archivos de sistema. Luego bastará con marcar todas las opciones disponibles y pedirle a la herramienta que borre todos esos archivos y carpetas. Ten en cuenta que no vaciará la carpeta por completo, ya que como hemos dicho, es una caché que sirve para reparar y actualizar aplicaciones instaladas. Pero es posible que el liberador de espacio encuentre archivos y carpetas de apps que desinstalaste pero que dejaron rastro.
A esta solución, que tendrás que realizar tú manualmente, le puedes añadir otra que es automática. Me refiero a la herramienta Sensor de almacenamiento, que encontrarás en Configuración de Windows si entras en Sistema y, a continuación, en Almacenamiento. Solo tienes que activar el sensor para que, por sí mismo, se encargue de la limpieza de archivos temporales y contenido en la nube cuando lo crea conveniente. Si entras dentro de sus opciones, tendrás ocasión de decirle cuándo activarse, cada cuántos días vaciar la papelera de reciclaje y cuándo eliminar la carpeta Descargas. También hay un botón para Ejecutar Sensor de almacenamiento ahora.
Aparte de estas dos soluciones, que son las más efectivas, hay más cosas que puedes hacer para obtener más espacio en disco sin tocar manualmente la carpeta Windows Installer. Por ejemplo, revisando las aplicaciones instaladas. En Configuración > Aplicaciones > Aplicaciones instaladas las tienes ordenadas por tamaño. Es posible que veas que alguna app o juego ocupan espacio y no los has abierto en semanas o meses.

articles.title: Discogs’ Kevin Lewandowski can’t live without his AeroPress
articles.text:
Twenty-five years ago, Kevin Lewandowski founded Discogs, arguably the destination online for obsessive vinyl collectors and music nerds of all stripes. It is a marketplace for buying and selling records, obviously, but it’s also become so much more. It’s a shockingly comprehensive database that covers not just albums and singles, but all the various versions and pressings. It’s a really fun rabbit hole to disappear down when you’re trying to figure out what obscure pressing of Ministry’s The Mind is a Terrible Thing to Taste or Psalm 69 you had in high school, because you definitely blasted the cover of “Lay Lady Lay” all the time and 100 percent never owned Filth Pig.
Discogs’ Kevin Lewandowski can’t live without his AeroPress
The founder of Discogs talks coffee, Rez, and (of course) records.
Discogs’ Kevin Lewandowski can’t live without his AeroPress
The founder of Discogs talks coffee, Rez, and (of course) records.
In the years since it debuted, Discogs has grown to be much more than just a site where audiophiles go to trade rare first pressings of Beach Boys records. There are forums, groups, user-created lists, and more. It’s part eBay, part Reddit, and IMDB — just specifically for music.
With more and more people turning their back on the algorithm and rediscovering physical media, now seemed like a perfect time to check in with Lewandowski.
What is your most indispensable tool?
My AeroPress. I use it multiple times a day. In fact, I just made a coffee with it [sips coffee].
How many tabs do you have open right now?
Probably around 30 on my work computer. My personal computer is worse — probably 40 or 50.
Which social media platform do you use the most?
I look at X and Instagram occasionally, but I don’t really post.
What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?
It’s not really a gadget, but I like to tinker. Lately I’ve been playing around with Home Assistant software and built my own setup to control things like the garage door and outdoor lights. So I guess my favorite gadget is one I made myself.
What is one thing you wish you had created?
Probably a game like Rez, which came out around 2000. It’s a rhythm game where you’re almost controlling the music as you play, about as close to DJing as a video game can get. I’ve actually had an idea for my own version with a similar concept. It’s still just an idea, though.
What do you do when you need to focus?
I’ll either clear everything off my desk or change locations completely. Go to a coffee shop or sit outside. Sometimes I just need a different environment.
What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?
Records. I was at Mint Gallery in Portland last week and picked up four. I still really like going into a record store and finding something to bring home. And I also recently picked up three reissues from the Moodsville / Acoustic Sounds series.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
The Secret Weapon.
What’s the last GIF or meme you used?
I don’t use memes very often, but one I was kind of proud of was putting a Discogs screen into a North Korean war room photo. I was advised that maybe it wasn’t one for the company chat.

articles.title: New Bluetooth High Data Throughput may finally satisfy audiophiles — Bluetooth HDT offers a maximum bandwidth of 7.5Mbps, allowing true lossless transmission
articles.text:
New Bluetooth High Data Throughput may finally satisfy audiophiles — Bluetooth HDT offers a maximum bandwidth of 7.5Mbps, allowing true lossless transmission
Audiophiles have always criticised Bluetooth, but HDT might finally be the convenient wireless experience they've needed.
The Bluetooth Special Interest Group (SIG) just announced the new Bluetooth High Data Throughput (HDT) feature on November 4, allowing a maximum bandwidth of 7.5 Mbps, almost 4x that of the previous Bluetooth LE 2M (2 Mbps). The new bandwidth is intended for high-bandwidth interactions between devices, such as AI, spatial computing, and even lossless audio transmission; the latter of which may finally satisfy audiophiles and their enjoyment of uncompressed audio.
Bluetooth HDT is Bluetooth’s new feature allowing for up to 7.5 Mbps of bandwidth. This new feature is needed by sophisticated modern devices that use a lot of data in their communication. It could be smartwatches, AI, or even extended reality (XR); less sophisticated but high-bandwidth, however, is lossless audio, which Bluetooth has never had enough bandwidth for, until HDT, that is.
Purists have long since criticized Bluetooth, but HDT may finally be the feature that satisfies them. Audiophiles have always preferred wired over Bluetooth, especially those who prefer lossless audio over compressed formats. Bluetooth LE 2M, even with its 2 Mbps bandwidth, cannot reliably transmit CD-quality 1.4 Mbps lossless audio, so it gets compressed through various means: SBC, AAC, aptX, LDAC, LC3, etc., and for audiophiles who want to listen to their lossless audio, compression is a downgrade to their experience, even if they likely can’t tell the difference between lossless and a high-quality 320kbps MP3 file.
However, HDT not only offers higher bandwidth but also improved reliability for consistent communication and uses even less power, as stated on Bluetooth’s feature enhancements page, which adds that HDT provides the capacity, efficiency, and wireless performance needed for high-resolution and lossless audio. As mentioned, CD lossless quality hovers around 0.8-1.4Mbps, while 24-bit 48 kHz is around 2.3 Mbps, and 24-bit 96 kHz is 4.6 Mbps, well under the maximum 7.5 Mbps bandwidth; only 24-bit 192 kHz exceeds it at 9.2 Mbps — but who is really able to tell the difference at that sampling rate?
It is worth noting that just because a device complies with the Bluetooth Core Specification 7.0, it doesn't mean that it automatically has the HDT feature, much less the maximum 7.5 Mbps feature. On page 2795 of the Core_v7.0 document (yes, I dug that far), it says that HDT2, HDT3, and HDT4 are required if HDT is featured, but HDT6 and HDT7.5 are optional. And it should be further noted that just because an audio device supports even the highest HDT7.5, it won’t immediately equate to a good experience, as tuning is also a big factor. With that said, HDT might make it possible for high-end wired audiophile favorites to get a wireless version.

articles.title: Enthusiast abandons self-hosted Microsoft Exchange after 27 years, moving mailboxes to Microsoft 365 — replaces final on-premises relay with Postfix, STARTTLS and Let's Encrypt certificates
articles.text:
Enthusiast abandons self-hosted Microsoft Exchange after 27 years, moving mailboxes to Microsoft 365 — replaces final on-premises relay with Postfix, STARTTLS, and Let's Encrypt certificates
Postfix replaces 27-year-old Microsoft Exchange server after mailbox migration to Microsoft 365
Running your own email server is one thing. Keeping it alive for nearly three decades is quite another. One homelab enthusiast has finally decided to call time on his Microsoft Exchange installation after maintaining it since 1999, replacing the last remaining server with Postfix on Ubuntu Server LTS. The user, posting as Meta4X on Reddit’s r/homelab on November 5, said they had already moved their mailboxes and email delivery to Microsoft 365 a couple of years ago. Exchange was still hanging around, however, serving as a relay for alerts generated by hardware and software on their local network. With that final job now being handed to Postfix, the 27-year run is coming to an end.
Meta4X’s installation began with Exchange 5.5 running on Windows NT 4. Since then, they have upgraded through Exchange 2000, 2003, 2007, 2010, 2013, 2016 and finally Exchange 2019. They said access to Microsoft’s software through MSDN, TechNet and the Microsoft Action Pack had allowed them to keep the setup running over the years. The end of support for Exchange 2019 last year was one reason to consider keeping the server around. Microsoft has since moved its on-premises Exchange platform to Exchange Server Subscription Edition (SE), which comes with ongoing licensing requirements. That said, the transition is not quite as straightforward as the original post suggests.
In the post, the Redditor shared a photo from 2003, when they upgraded from Exchange 2000 to Exchange 2003. The server did not have a conventional PC case, and its motherboard was strapped to the cardboard box it came with using zip ties.
One commenter pointed out that existing Exchange 2019 licenses can be used with Exchange SE under qualifying licensing arrangements. Meta4X admitted that they did not know that, adding that they were probably better off not knowing. “I did not know that, thank you! In hindsight, I'm glad I wasn't aware because I probably would have put off killing Exchange,” they wrote. In other words, the server was not necessarily being retired because there was no way to keep it licensed. The move gave its owner an opportunity to finally get rid of a system that had outlived its original purpose.
For context, the replacement is Postfix, an open-source mail transfer agent that will run on Ubuntu Server LTS. The enthusiast is also using the migration to address several pieces of technical debt that have accumulated during the server’s long life. “Moving to Postfix is a good opportunity to implement STARTTLS, move to Let's Encrypt certificates, implement boot encryption, and eliminate a bunch of other technical debt that has accumulated over the past 20+ years,” Meta4X explained.
STARTTLS upgrades an ordinary SMTP connection to an encrypted TLS connection, while Let’s Encrypt provides publicly trusted certificates that can be renewed automatically. Boot encryption adds another layer of protection by securing data on the system drive. These are planned improvements, though — the Reddit post does not establish that the new configuration is already fully deployed. Meanwhile, Postfix is hardly the only destination for Exchange refugees. Several commentators said they had moved Mailcow, while another recommended Grommunio as an alternative for people who still want to keep their mail infrastructure on-premises. Others were more than happy to leave email hosting to Microsoft and other cloud providers.
That said, the move to Postfix does not necessarily make email security a solved problem. Postfix’s own documentation explains that enabling TLS can encrypt SMTP sessions, but administrators still need to configure certificate handling and decide how connections should behave when a remote server does not support encryption. We have previously reported on a vulnerability in Exim that exposed millions of email servers, showing how flaws in mail transfers can put systems at risk. Ransomware has particularly been a headache, exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft Exchange. A more recent report highlights how Outlook silently falls back to unencrypted email connections

articles.title: Cet astronaute canadien capture une photo vertigineuse à 400 kilomètres au-dessus de la Terre
articles.text:
Nous voyons des photos de sorties dans l’espace, en dehors de la Station spatiale internationale (ISS), depuis plus de 25 ans. On finirait presque par s’y habituer. Pourtant, celle que Joshua Kutryk a publiée sur son compte X, juste après sa sortie spatiale du jeudi 5 novembre 2026, donne franchement le vertige.
Entre l’astronaute et la Terre, à environ 400 kilomètres plus bas, il n’y a rien d’autre que le câble qui le retient à la station. « Les pieds qui pendent au-dessus de la Terre à une vitesse de 28 000 km/h. Ne pas regarder en bas ! (C’est une blague — je regarde définitivement vers le bas, car la Terre est tout simplement magnifique) », commente Joshua Kutryk.
Joshua Kutryk, colonel de l’Aviation royale canadienne, a été recruté par l’Agence spatiale canadienne en 2017. Le 1er octobre 2026, il a décollé avec la mission Crew-13 de SpaceX. Le 29 octobre, il est devenu le cinquième Canadien à sortir dans l’espace. Le lendemain, il a parlé à la presse d’une « surcharge sensorielle », selon Canadian Geographic : « Votre esprit ne sait pas quoi faire de cette image. »
Sept heures dehors pour finir le chantier électrique de l’ISS
D’après le blog de la NASA consacré à l’ISS, Joshua Kutryk et l’Américain Anil Menon ont passé 6 heures et 59 minutes à installer puis à déployer le huitième et dernier panneau IROSA, un panneau solaire qui arrive enroulé et se déroule une fois fixé à la station. Le chantier avait commencé en février 2021 et a demandé 18 sorties au total. La station peut désormais produire environ 215 kilowatts d’électricité, contre 160 avant, soit un tiers de plus.
Ces heures dehors usent le corps. Après sa troisième sortie, l’astronaute française Sophie Adenot a eu cette phrase révélatrice : « Rien que de tenir un stylo est douloureux. » De retour sur Terre, elle a aussi raconté comment son corps avait vécu l’espace. Dehors, chaque geste demande en plus une grande attention, car perdre un outil dans le vide est l’une des hantises des astronautes.
Pour Joshua Kutryk, l’aventure continue : sa mission dure six mois, et il doit donc rester à bord de l’ISS jusqu’au printemps 2027.

articles.title: Pour chasser l'humidité dans une petite pièce, on a testé le déshumidificateur Duux Bora 12L
articles.text:
| Capacité de déshumidification | 12 L / jour | 
| Surface couverte | 30 m2 | 
| Capacité du réservoir | 1.7 L | 
| Dimensions | 434 x 256 x 203 mm | 
| Poids | 9.5 kg | 
| Montage sur roulettes | Oui | 
| Évacuation continue | Oui | 
| Connecté | Non | 
Le Duux Bora 12L reprend le design du 20L dans un format plus compact, mais abandonne le wifi. Avec deux vitesses et un mode Buanderie, il s'adresse aux petits espaces humides. Nous avons évalué sa prise en main et ses performances.
Après le Bora 20L, Duux décline son déshumidificateur dans une version plus compacte. Le Bora 12L DXDH12 reprend les grandes lignes de son aîné, mais réduit sa capacité d'extraction à 12 l par jour pour une surface allant jusqu'à 30 m². Il vise donc plutôt une chambre, un bureau ou une buanderie qu'un grand espace ouvert.
Cette réduction de format s'accompagne de quelques concessions. Le réservoir passe ainsi de 4 à 1,7 l et la connexion wifi disparaît. Le pilotage s'effectue dès lors entièrement depuis le panneau de commandes. L'appareil conserve toutefois deux vitesses de ventilation, plusieurs modes de fonctionnement et un filtre à charbon actif.
La parenté avec le Bora 20L saute aux yeux avec une coque blanche aux angles arrondis et le même dessus noir regroupant les commandes et la sortie d'air. Le 12L se contente toutefois de 43,4 cm de haut, 25,6 cm de large et 20,3 cm de profondeur. Ce faible encombrement permet donc de lui trouver assez facilement une place.
Avec 9,5 kg sur la balance, il se manipule plus facilement que les 14,5 kg du 20L. Sa grande poignée rabattable facilite le transport d'une pièce à l'autre et les roulettes permettent de le déplacer sans le soulever.
La grille supérieure souffle vers le haut. Elle n'est pas démontable et n’autorise pas d'orienter le flux à sa guise. À l'arrière, la grille d'admission se retire pour accéder au filtre à charbon actif fourni. Pour l'entretien, on enlève le filtre à charbon avant de rincer son support, puis on laisse sécher avant de remonter l'ensemble.
Le réservoir se retire par l'avant dans la partie basse. Une fenêtre permet de surveiller le niveau et sa prise en main est pratique pour aller le vider. En revanche, ses 1,7 l imposent des allers-retours plus fréquents lorsque l'humidité est importante. Une sécurité interrompt la déshumidification quand le bac est plein.
Le tuyau fourni se raccorde à la sortie de drainage arrière pour éviter ces vidanges. Sa longueur reste pourtant modeste et il faudra placer l'appareil près de l'évacuation ou prévoir un tuyau adapté plus long. Gare, l’eau s'écoulant par gravité, le trajet doit rester descendant. Duux a aussi prévu des supports arrière pour enrouler le cordon secteur.
Ici, pas d'appairage ni d'app à installer. Les commandes tactiles placées sur le dessus suffisent à mettre le Bora 12L en route et choisir son fonctionnement. L'afficheur central indique le taux d'humidité mesuré, puis laisse temporairement la place à la valeur que l'on règle.
En mode automatique, l'hygrostat permet de sélectionner une consigne de 30 à 80 % par paliers de 5 %. Le compresseur extrait l'humidité jusqu'à atteindre la valeur demandée, tandis que la ventilation conserve la vitesse sélectionnée. La notice précise que le ventilateur continue de tourner lorsque le compresseur s'arrête.
Le mode Continu maintient l'extraction sans chercher à respecter un taux d'humidité défini. Pour le linge, un appui prolongé sur la touche dédiée active le mode Buanderie, qui associe la ventilation maximale à une minuterie de 4 h. On dispose aussi d'une minuterie d'arrêt réglable de 1 à 24 h et d'un verrouillage des commandes.
Le mode Nuit mérite une précision, déjà valable sur le Bora 20L. Il agit en effet sur les lumières et les bips, pas sur le bruit de fonctionnement. L'éclairage diminue, puis l'affichage et les voyants s'éteignent après 10 s, à l'exception du témoin de ce mode. Pour limiter le souffle, il faut donc choisir soi-même la petite vitesse.
Enfin, une fonction d'autonettoyage lance un cycle de séchage d'environ 1 h. Duux recommande de l'utiliser tous les trois mois et avant un rangement prolongé. L'absence de connexion prive cette version du suivi de l'humidité et de la programmation à distance du 20L.
Nous avons utilisé le Bora 12L dans une pièce d'environ 10 m², ouverte sur le reste du logement. L'appareil a bien réduit l'humidité selon nos deux outils de mesures, la station météo Netatmo et l'analyseur Airthings View Plus, mais la diminution a fini par plafonner.
Cette observation invite à le réserver en priorité aux pièces modestes et fermées, plutôt qu'à lui demander d'assécher tout un logement depuis un couloir. Une petite buanderie constitue notamment un usage cohérent avec son format et son mode dédié au séchage du linge.
Le bilan sonore est plutôt acceptable pour la catégorie. À 2 m de distance, nous avons relevé 38 dB en petite vitesse et 41 dB à la ventilation maximale. Dans les mêmes conditions de distance, nous avions mesuré respectivement 40 et 47 dB sur le Bora 20L. Le petit modèle est donc plus discret, surtout à pleine vitesse.
Il reste audible dans une pièce calme, mais la ventilation minimale rend sa présence supportable en journée. Pour une chambre, mieux vaudra le faire fonctionner avant le coucher ou accepter un bruit de fond pendant la nuit.
Le Duux Bora 12L conserve les qualités pratiques du 20L dans un format plus facile à déplacer et loger. Ses commandes sont simples, sa poignée et ses roulettes facilitent les déplacements, tandis que le niveau sonore reste raisonnable à petite vitesse. L'extraction montre toutefois ses limites dans un espace ouvert et mieux vaut lui confier une pièce modeste et fermée. Son réservoir de 1,7 l demande aussi des vidanges régulières, sauf à utiliser le drainage continu. Pour une petite buanderie ou un besoin ponctuel de déshumidification, ce Bora est un appareil accessible à l'usage et peu encombrant.
Le Comfee Aqua Dry 12 mise sur un budget contenu avec une capacité d'extraction comparable, un réservoir plus généreux de 2,5 l et un mode Silent qui réduit effectivement la ventilation. Le Duux Bora 20L offre davantage de capacité d'extraction, un bac de 4 l et une application pour le pilotage à distance et le suivi de l'humidité, au prix cependant d'un encombrement et d'un poids supérieurs.

articles.title: NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake
articles.text:
Around 7PM each weeknight, I find myself standing in front of the fridge, trying to decide on something for dinner that won’t make my husband complain, “Chicken again?” Yes, I should meal plan more, but I don’t, so this is where I’m at. A nightly battle in which the chicken usually wins.
NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake
I tested the new AI-powered tool on ingredient swaps, recipe scaling, and a missing Bundt pan.
Recently, my best weapon in this fight has been AI. Between Alexa Plus in the Echo smart display on my kitchen counter, the Samsung Food app on my fridge, and even an AI-powered cooking robot, AI has become my go-to sous chef — albeit one I need to keep a close eye on. It’s helped me swap ingredients, generate ideas, fix things when I mess up, and yes, even cook better. So I was intrigued when my go-to recipe app, NYT Cooking, introduced an AI assistant.
Many, including some NYT Cooking users and recipe purists, are skeptical of this new tool (available to subscribers on iOS only at launch), and I get why. One of the things I like most about NYT Cooking is that it features thousands of recipes from dozens of reputable sources — such as the New York Times archives, restaurants, cookbooks, and food columnists — and real people have tested them. (I’ve tried some purely AI-generated recipes and they were not good).
Another great feature of the service, which I’ve been paying for for several years, is the reader comments. Here, I’ve often found solutions to cooking dilemmas, like what to substitute for makrut lime leaves — there’s always one slightly bougie ingredient in an NYT Cooking recipe that I don’t have on hand.
However, reading through hundreds of comments to find answers at 7PM on a weeknight isn’t always practical. And this is where I’ve found the NYT Cooking assistant helpful. Among other things, it was trained on user comments, and in my few days testing it, it provided practical substitutions and solid cooking guidance for the new ingredients. It also won’t unquestionably agree to crazy requests (I tried!). As with all AI tools, it’s not perfect — it almost made me put half the required butter in my cake — but as a tool, it is useful and feels like a solid application of AI. Importantly, it doesn’t change the existing recipe; it leaves it as is and creates a new one for you.
It doesn’t change the existing recipe; it leaves it as is and creates a new one for you
The assistant appears in the app in a small text box on the recipe page with a prompt: “Customize this recipe…” From here, you type in a question to adapt it to your needs. This can be as simple as “What can I substitute for this ingredient?” to “Scale this recipe to feed seven people, and make it vegan and gluten-free.” The New York Times has also said the feature can suggest substitutions for cooking equipment and convert measurements; the latter option has been in the app for a couple of years.
Last Friday night, instead of staring aimlessly into the fridge, I turned to the Chicken folder in my NYT Cooking app Recipe Box and found a One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger I’d been wanting to try. Only I didn’t have chicken thighs or half the ingredients.
I could have figured these steps myself, but it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible.
I typed my dilemma into the assistant box on the recipe page: “I have chicken tenders, fresh ginger, garlic, rice, broth, limes, but no chard or cilantro or scallions. I do have green beans and red onions.” Within seconds, it created a new version of the recipe, with a new title: One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger and Green Beans. It suggested a shorter browning time for the tenders, cooking the red onion alongside the chicken, and steaming the green beans on top of the rice for the last eight minutes instead of the chard. Every change was highlighted in the new recipe under a Your Version tab, and I could flip back to the original at any point.
I noticed it hadn’t adjusted for the lack of cilantro, saying it was optional. So I asked if I could use Thai basil, which I happen to have, and it agreed, highlighting how it would change the flavor. While I could have figured out a lot of these steps myself, maybe with the help of Google, it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible and nice not to have to swipe out of the app. The NYT Cooking editors say it’s been trained not to comply with requests that will taste bad.
The resulting dish — which took the same amount of time to cook as the original — was delicious and got my husband’s seal of approval (he just had the leftovers for lunch). It was very different from the recipe Yasmin Fahr wrote, and I can see the purists’ point. But the rewritten recipe was much easier to use and produced a better dish than winging it with my own subs gleaned from the comments section, which I usually do with varying degrees of success.
I cook regularly, so I had a sense of what ingredients I had on hand that might work for the dish I wanted to make. But the assistant can also help if you have no idea what to use as a substitute. For example, I was cooking a Thai red curry and asked what I could use instead of makrut lime leaf. It replied, saying that grated lime zest would work, but “it misses the deeper floral, herbal aroma” of fresh limes. (See? Bougie.)
Over the weekend, I tried several more swaps, asking whether half-and-half would work instead of cream in a caramel apple Dutch baby, or if Castelvetrano olives and smoked paprika could stand in for kalamata and chile pepper in a roasted halibut dish. Swapping spices is always a bold move in any dish, as it can really ruin the flavor.
I also had the app convert the Dutch baby recipe’s metric weights to US measurements, which it did seamlessly. Then I threw in some curveballs. How about using fresh cayenne peppers with the halibut? It warned me that substituting cayenne for chile “brings significant, sharp heat.” Could I swap ladyfingers for minced beef in this trifle (à la Rachel Green in Friends)? “Minced beef cannot be used in place of the ladyfingers or anywhere in this sweet dessert trifle.” Good call.
While I was cooking, I compared the NYT Cooking assistant with Alexa Plus, Amazon’s generative-AI voice assistant I regularly use to help me cook via the Echo Show 11 smart display in my kitchen. Interestingly, it offered the same guidance as the Cooking assistant on substitutions for the chicken and rice dish, but with slightly different cooking times. Alexa pulls some recipes from the NYT app through a partnership between the companies.
However, Alexa couldn’t show the modified recipe on its screen; it could only tell me the changes while showing the original. When I asked it to walk me through them, it got confused and improvised, telling me to cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces — which wasn’t in the modified recipe. Overall, I found using the Cooking app more reliable, although messier. It would be great to be able to use voice control to navigate the app, as I can with Alexa on my smart display, rather than using my garlicky fingers.
Time for a bigger challenge: baking.
I am typically not a baker. My cakes come out flat, and my cookies don’t crumble. Even the smart mixer I tested a few years ago couldn’t save me. I also rarely have the right equipment. So I took Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake, a recipe by NYT Cooking editor Genevieve Ko (who announced the AI feature), and asked it to turn it into muffins. (Who has a Bundt cake pan?!)
It modified the recipe’s cooking time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. But that was going to make 24 muffins, way too many for me. So I asked it to halve the recipe to get 12 muffins. This led to some smart choices, like halving five eggs to three instead of an unhelpful two and a half.
For science, I bought a Bundt pan to make the original version too. Both turned out great, but things got a bit sticky when I swapped between the original recipe and the AI version in the app. You can’t save your new recipe separately, which caused confusion when I was cooking the original. Instead of scrolling back through the recipe with sticky fingers, I asked the assistant how much butter I needed (using voice typing), and it gave me the modified recipe’s 6 tablespoons rather than the original’s three-quarter cup, without telling me which version it was using. You can delete your version, which I would advise doing to avoid issues like this — 6 tablespoons of butter would have made for a dry cake.
If you already read all the comments before starting a New York Times recipe, then you will probably find this tool offers a similar experience in a more streamlined way. For everyday problems — wrong cut of chicken, no cilantro, or no Bundt cake pan — it was genuinely helpful and saved me a trip to the store. It was also smart enough to know when to say no to minced beef in a trifle.
As with every AI tool I’ve used in the kitchen, the NYT Cooking AI assistant works well as a sous chef, but it’s not the head chef — I still felt the need to double-check amounts and cooking times and cross-reference them with the original to make sure it hadn’t done something outlandish.
If you’re a purist, you can just ignore the assistant. While you can’t turn off the chat box, it’s easy to scroll past. I do think it will make me use the app more often, since I no longer need to worry as much when I don’t have makrut lime leaves on hand or the right cut of meat. For me, standing in front of the fridge with chicken tenders and no plan, it’s been a useful addition to my nightly cooking routine.
Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: Meta adia regras sobre coleta de conteúdo jornalístico para treinar IA
articles.text:
A Meta adiou a implementação de novas regras de coleta e uso de dados (leia-se: conteúdo) publicado por veículos de comunicação. As regras cobriam também o desenvolvimento e treinamento de sistemas de inteligência artificial (IA).
Em comunicado, a big tech informou o seguinte: “Recentemente, anunciamos a atualização dos Termos Comerciais da Meta, dos Termos do Catálogo de Produtos, dos Termos para Criação de Anúncios com Autoatendimento e dos Termos de IA Generativa para Criativo do Anúncio. Essas atualizações estão pausadas e não entrarão em vigor em 20 de novembro de 2026.”
“Seguimos em diálogo com as partes interessadas e compartilharemos novas informações assim que possível. Enquanto isso, nossos termos existentes permanecem em vigor”, acrescenta a empresa no texto.
Justiça de São Paulo proíbe Meta de usar conteúdo jornalístico sem licença para treinar IA
O comunicado da Meta vem pouco depois de um revés judicial no Brasil. Na terça-feira (03), a Justiça de São Paulo concedeu uma liminar atendendo a uma ação movida pela Associação Nacional de Jornais (ANJ), Associação Brasileira de Emissoras de Rádio e Televisão (Abert) e Associação Nacional de Editores de Revistas (ANER).
Em suma, a decisão proibiu a Meta de coletar e usar sem autorização conteúdos jornalísticos de veículos ligados a essas três associações.
A proibição previa multa diária de R$ 1 milhão em caso de descumprimento, limitada a R$ 100 milhões.
A decisão da Justiça de São Paulo também obrigava a Meta a manter ativas as contas dos veículos de comunicação que não permitissem a coleta e o uso do seu conteúdo, sem nenhum tipo de punição.
O caso não é isolado. Nos Estados Unidos, por exemplo, a Meta recebeu cartas de um senador republicano e de um senador democrata criticando as novas regras.
Na Noruega, a nova política foi suspensa por uma liminar num processo movido por empresas de mídia.
No Reino Unido, a big tech é alvo de uma investigação. A Autoridade de Concorrência e Mercados apura se as exigências contratuais da Meta configuram abuso de posição dominante ou imposição de condições comerciais desleais a veículos de comunicação e anunciantes.
O Olhar Digital conversou sobre a decisão da Justiça de São Paulo com dois especialistas: Antonielle Freitas, pós-graduada em Direito Digital pela Escola Brasileira de Direito (EBD) e membro da Comissão Especial de Privacidade e Proteção de Dados da OAB/SP; e Marcelo Inoue Cárgano, formado em Direito pela USP e pós-graduando em Direito Digital pelo ITS-UERJ.
Confira os destaques das entrevistas nesta matéria.
Pedro Spadoni é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de Piracicaba. Já escreveu para sites, revistas e jornal.

articles.title: Ce site rétro affiche la météo d'aujourd'hui comme une télé des années 1990, musique d'ascenseur comprise
articles.text:
Aux États-Unis, toute une génération a grandi avec les « Local on the 8s ». The Weather Channel, une chaîne câblée lancée en 1982, diffusait ces bulletins météo locaux toutes les 10 minutes, sur fond de smooth jazz. Depuis le 1er avril 2026, ces bulletins sont de retour sur RetroCast Now, un site gratuit que la chaîne avait alors présenté en vidéo sur Instagram, en précisant qu’il ne s’agissait même pas d’un poisson d’avril.
Ce vendredi 6 novembre, The Weather Channel l’a remis en avant dans un message sur X, qui semble répondre à une publication de Brian Roemmele, un entrepreneur américain très suivi sur le réseau, qui avait partagé quelques jours plus tôt un autre projet semblable.
Un décor de 1995, des prévisions météo d’aujourd’hui
À l’époque, ces écrans étaient fabriqués par les WeatherStar, des boîtiers installés chez les câblo-opérateurs qui inséraient les prévisions locales dans le programme national. RetroCast Now en reprend tout le décor : conditions actuelles, prévisions à 36 heures et sur plusieurs jours, carte régionale, phases de la Lune, polices pixelisées et musique d’ascenseur.
Numerama a pu vérifier qu’il est bien possible d’afficher des prévisions en français, dans notre cas pour la ville de Paris. Attention, toutefois, notez que les prévisions de températures sont indiquées en degrés Fahrenheit — ambiance USA jusqu’au bout !
C’est le développeur et designer indépendant Lee Martin qui a codé le site. Il a présenté le projet sur X et sur Instagram, en rappelant que des fans avaient déjà bricolé leurs propres émulateurs de WeatherStar. Sa version, elle, prend ses données directement chez The Weather Channel. Les prévisions valent donc celles de weather.com (et oui, avec probablement les erreurs que fait toute prévision météo).
De quoi remplacer l’application Météo de l’iPhone, souvent prise en défaut, le temps d’un bulletin nostalgique.

articles.title: China acaba de conseguir algo extraordinario en su estación espacial: ha enfriado átomos hasta un récord histórico
articles.text:
El frío tiene un límite que la física conoce muy bien, pero al que ningún laboratorio puede llegar exactamente: el cero absoluto. Cuanto más nos acercamos a él, más difícil resulta reducir la energía térmica de los átomos, hasta el punto de que cada pequeño descenso de temperatura representa un desafío experimental. Y lo interesante no es solo alcanzar una cifra extraordinariamente baja, sino lo que sucede con la materia en esas condiciones. A temperaturas tan extremas, comienzan a manifestarse fenómenos cuánticos que normalmente permanecen ocultos por la agitación térmica.
Desde la órbita terrestre, un equipo de científicos chinos ha dado un nuevo paso hacia ese límite. Los investigadores han obtenido en la estación espacial Tiangong una nube de unos 20.000 átomos de rubidio con una temperatura cinética equivalente de 9,7 picokelvin, según un estudio publicado en Science. Hablamos de apenas 9,7 billonésimas de kelvin por encima del cero absoluto, situado en −273,15 °C. Para conseguirlo, trabajaron con un condensado de Bose-Einstein, un estado de la materia en el que numerosos átomos comparten un mismo estado cuántico. No han creado un elemento nuevo, sino preparado materia conocida en unas condiciones extraordinarias.
El equipo recurrió a un procedimiento que combina distintas técnicas de enfriamiento atómico. Primero utilizó haces de luz láser para mantener los átomos confinados en una trampa óptica y aplicó el llamado enfriamiento evaporativo, que permite escapar a los más energéticos y reduce la energía media de los restantes. Después, los investigadores trasladaron los átomos a otra configuración óptica y debilitaron progresivamente su confinamiento, siguiendo un procedimiento de enfriamiento en dos etapas. La última fase, descrita como expansión no adiabática, contribuyó a reducir todavía más la energía asociada al movimiento de la nube.
Por qué el espacio ha sido clave para conseguir este récord
La elección del espacio no fue casual. En la Tierra, la gravedad limita tanto la posibilidad de mantener los átomos en trampas muy débiles como el tiempo disponible para observarlos después de liberarlos. Según explica la Universidad de Pekín, las condiciones de microgravedad de Tiangong permitieron reducir la intensidad del confinamiento y estudiar la expansión libre de la nube durante siete segundos. La velocidad a la que se dispersan los átomos permite determinar su temperatura cinética equivalente. De ahí procede la cifra comunicada, que no corresponde a la temperatura del laboratorio espacial ni significa que la nube permaneciera confinada durante esos siete segundos.
El resultado adquiere otra dimensión cuando lo comparamos con los antecedentes científicos. En 2021, un equipo alemán alcanzó una temperatura equivalente de 38 picokelvin mediante un experimento en una torre de caída libre, detalla una publicación en Physical Review Letters. La nueva marca china equivale aproximadamente a una cuarta parte de aquel valor, aunque los investigadores comunican una incertidumbre de +3,2 y −2,7 picokelvin sobre su estimación central de 9,7. La NASA también lleva años estudiando gases cuánticos en la Estación Espacial Internacional, donde ya se habían producido condensados de Bose-Einstein. Conviene, eso sí, distinguir las técnicas utilizadas y las magnitudes medidas en cada experimento.
Detrás de este avance también hay un enorme desafío de ingeniería. Según el Instituto de Óptica y Mecánica Fina de Shanghái, perteneciente a la Academia China de Ciencias, los estudios de viabilidad del proyecto comenzaron en 2011 y el sistema experimental llegó a la estación espacial en 2022, a bordo del módulo Mengtian. Para hacerlo posible, los investigadores tuvieron que integrar las capacidades de un laboratorio terrestre de unos 20 metros cúbicos y 10 toneladas en un instrumento espacial de apenas 0,7 metros cúbicos y 500 kilos. Todo ello exigió combinar sistemas de vacío ultraalto, láseres de alta potencia y mecanismos de control capaces de mantener la estabilidad y precisión necesarias para estos experimentos.
¿Y para qué sirve acercarse tanto a ese límite? Según los investigadores participantes, disponer de gases ultrafríos y observar su evolución durante más tiempo abre nuevas posibilidades para estudiar cómo interactúan las partículas y cómo se comportan los sistemas cuánticos. También podría contribuir al desarrollo de interferómetros atómicos, instrumentos que aprovechan las propiedades ondulatorias de los átomos para realizar mediciones de gran precisión. Entre las líneas de investigación que se plantean figura incluso la búsqueda de determinadas formas hipotéticas de materia oscura, aunque todavía hablamos de posibilidades futuras, no de aplicaciones demostradas.

articles.title: Por dentro da dublagem de games no Brasil: de The Outlaws, em 1997, às vozes de Kratos e Cyberpunk 2077
articles.text:
Ouvir personagens de videogame falando português brasileiro nem sempre foi comum. Durante muito tempo, a maioria dos jogos chegava ao país apenas em inglês ou japonês, tornando o idioma uma barreira para parte do público.
Um dos primeiros marcos dessa trajetória foi Outlaws, lançado pela LucasArts em 1997, que recebeu dublagem em português brasileiro. Na época, localizar completamente as vozes de um jogo ainda era uma iniciativa pouco frequente.
A situação começou a mudar nas décadas seguintes, especialmente com o crescimento do mercado brasileiro e a chegada de grandes produções totalmente localizadas.
De Kratos a Geralt: as vozes que marcaram os games
A expansão da dublagem trouxe personagens que passaram a ser associados às vozes de atores brasileiros.
Em God of War, Ricardo Juarez assumiu a interpretação de Kratos a partir de God of War: Ascension, em 2013, e retornou no jogo de 2018. Já The Last of Us contou com Luiz Carlos Persy como Joel e Luiza Caspary como Ellie.
Outros exemplos incluem Sérgio Moreno como Geralt em The Witcher 3, Tatiane Keplmair como Aloy em Horizon Zero Dawn e Wendel Bezerra como Markus em Detroit: Become Human.
Em produções mais recentes, como Cyberpunk 2077, a localização brasileira também passou a acompanhar narrativas extensas, com numerosos personagens e diálogos.
Dublar um jogo vai além de traduzir
O trabalho envolve tradução, adaptação de roteiro, direção e interpretação. Diferentemente de filmes, os atores nem sempre recebem as cenas completas como referência, o que pode tornar o processo mais complexo.
Além da imersão, a dublagem amplia a acessibilidade linguística, permitindo que jogadores acompanhem histórias sem depender exclusivamente de legendas ou do conhecimento de outros idiomas.
De Outlaws aos grandes RPGs contemporâneos, a evolução da dublagem mostra como o português brasileiro deixou de ser uma exceção para se tornar parte importante da experiência de jogar.
Rachele Victoria é formada em Letras, MBA em Inovação e atua há 10 anos com comunicação e conteúdo gamer.
Amazon Prime também é feito para jogadores!
