articles.title: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
articles.text:
Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way:
The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies.
Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company.
What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips.
Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

articles.title: In the software factory, engineers become process engineers
articles.text:
In the software factory, engineers become process engineers
For most of software’s history, the scarce resource was people who could write code. Every process the industry built assumed it. Sprints, code review, staging, and release trains were all designed around humans doing the work by hand.
That assumption is gone. By September, more than 40% of pull requests on GitHub started with an agent’s first draft, up from 17% in March. Work is moving to machines, but the process around it hasn’t caught up.
Agents made generating code cheap and fast. For the most part, they have not yet had the same impact on shipping it. CircleCI’s 2026 delivery data showed average daily workflow runs grew 59% year over year, with the top 5% of teams up 97% and the bottom quartile showing no measurable increase. A study of one company that mandated doubling pull request output found that load per reviewer doubled and automated review overtook human review in coverage within months.
“When work gets automated in any industry, the people don’t disappear. They stop doing the work and start designing the system the work runs through.”
When work gets automated in any industry, the people don’t disappear. Their job changes. They stop doing the work and start designing the system the work runs through. Software engineers are becoming process engineers, and what they build is a software factory.
Three manufacturing lessons carry over to agents
Software is not a car plant. A factory builds the same product thousands of times, and software never ships the same change twice. But three ideas carry over, because they are about running a system where machines do the work.
The first is that people design the system, not the output. Ford’s Model T went from 12.5 hours per car to one every 93 minutes by 1914, and the workers did not get eight times faster. Engineers redesigned the line.
Second, quality gets built in at every step. Sakichi Toyoda invented a loom that stopped automatically when any thread broke, so one operator could run many machines instead of watching one. Toyota built its production system around that idea, and W. Edwards Deming spent decades telling manufacturers to stop relying on end-of-line inspection.
The third is that the slowest step sets the pace. That was Eliyahu Goldratt’s point in “The Goal.” Speed up any step other than the bottleneck, and you pile up work in front of it. Agents sped up coding, and the pile is now in review and verification.
A software factory is a network of agents
A software factory runs on many specialized agents, each good at one job, passing work to others across the lifecycle. A research agent turns usage data and customer calls into a brief, and a spec agent writes requirements with acceptance criteria. A coding agent writes the change, and a review agent reviews the change. A test agent runs the change and sends failures back, and a release agent rolls it out behind feature flags. A site reliability engineering (SRE) agent triages what breaks in production and opens the next piece of work.
Most handoffs in that loop are agent-to-agent, and that changes what a handoff is. Between humans, a handoff can be a Slack thread and some shared context. Between agents, it has to be a contract that states what gets passed, in what shape, and with what proof. A spec without acceptance criteria gives the coding agent nothing to aim at, and a change without test evidence gives the release agent nothing to trust.
“A spec without acceptance criteria gives the coding agent nothing to aim at, and a change without test evidence gives the release agent nothing to trust.”
Agent-to-agent work also fails in new ways. Errors compound, because each agent builds on the last one’s output. Agents can agree too easily, or loop forever trading the same fix back and forth. A factory of agents needs what a factory of machines needs: checks between the stations, and someone who decides where those checks go.
Software engineers become process engineers
That someone is the software engineer. The job moves from writing code to designing the system that writes, tests, and ships it. That is more technical, not less, because you are now responsible for how all the code gets made. The work comes down to four jobs, and the first is designing the flow: which agents exist, what each one owns, what runs in parallel, and what each handoff must contain.
The second is defining good. An agent can’t hit a target nobody wrote down. Specs, acceptance criteria, performance budgets, and API contracts used to live in people’s heads. Now they have to be explicit enough for a machine to check.
The third is improving the line. When an agent ships a bug, the useful question is not why the agent did that but why the line let it through. Every escaped defect is a process bug.
The fourth is placing the human gates. Humans belong where a mistake is expensive, and the call takes judgment. Line-by-line human review of every agent pull request is a craft-era habit, the factory equivalent of hand-inspecting every bolt.
“When an agent ships a bug, the useful question is not why the agent did that but why the line let it through. Every escaped defect is a process bug.”
Agents write code and fix tests. A schema migration is costly to get wrong but cheap for a machine to check, so agents run it behind hard checks. User interface (UI) copy tastes but is cheap to change, so a human reviews it after it ships. What to build and where a security boundary sits gets a human gate.
Quality gets built into every change, not inspected at the end
Most teams still run the old model of quality assurance. Changes pile up, then go through one inspection at the end: a shared staging environment and a human reviewer. That is a single test bench for the whole plant, and once agents multiply the number of changes, it becomes the bottleneck Goldratt described.
Toyoda’s loom freed the operator because it checked every thread as it ran and stopped the moment one broke. Agent-written code needs the same mechanism. In a working software factory, the test agent checks every change as it is made, the coding agent fixes what fails, and nothing moves until it passes.
That check only means something if it runs where the failure would show up. Mocks don’t count, because they tell you a change works in a world that doesn’t exist. They were a stopgap that made sense when the pace of change was slow and standing up a production-like environment for every change was hard.
So, each change gets its own environment that behaves like production, with the services, databases, and APIs it will meet after release. A human only sees the change if it hits a gate, and by then it already works, with the evidence attached.
That model needs a test station for every change, cheap enough to use on every attempt. In practice, that means an environment that comes up in seconds, deploys only what the change touched and shares everything else so that you can verify the change end to end before merge.
Guardrails belong in the line, not in the prompt
Verification catches mistakes. Guardrails stop the ones that would cost too much to catch late. Assume agents will do anything the line allows, and design the line so that everything it allows is safe.
Manufacturing calls this error-proofing. You don’t put up a sign telling workers to insert the part the right way. You build a fixture that fits only one way. For agents, an instruction in a prompt is a sign on the wall, and a permission boundary is a fixture.
So each agent holds only the access its station needs, and the coding agent never holds production credentials. Every run is isolated, so one agent’s test can’t corrupt another’s. Required checks are enforced, every release can roll back on its own, and when a check can’t run, the change stops.
A line that quietly skips a broken inspection is worse than no inspection, because everyone believes it’s working. Agent-to-agent work adds one more rule: trust doesn’t pass down the chain. A review agent approving a change shouldn’t widen what the release agent can do.
Judgment stays human, and it becomes most of the job
Factories didn’t get rid of engineers. They created industrial engineering. You can’t design a line for work you don’t understand, so the best factory builders will be engineers who know what good code, good tests, and a safe rollout look like from doing it by hand.
Some work stays off the line. The first version of something new, a strange production bug, and a design nobody has tried are bench work. They stay hands-on until they are understood well enough to standardize.
Some decisions never move to a machine: what’s worth building, what a customer means rather than what they said, when to trade speed for risk and who answers for what ships. Those were always the hard part of the job. Now they’re most of it.
The best process wins, not the best model
Agents made code cheap, and every team can reach for the same models. What separates the teams pulling ahead is the line they build around those agents, with contracts between stations, human gates where judgment matters, and verification on every change. Designing that line is now the software engineer’s job. We built Signadot to give every change its own test station, and it is a practical place to start building yours.

articles.title: Microsoft patent filing describes AI that rewrites what people say in livestreams in real time
articles.text:
The takeaway: Microsoft, Sony, and other companies have filed several patents in the past year that use generative AI to alter content in real time. Patents don't always become products, but the frequency of the filings demonstrates strong interest in real-time AI editing. Microsoft says its latest patent is only for cleaning up and translating broadcasts, but the basic concept raises concerns about accuracy and misinformation.
AI-edited and AI-generated videos have been among the most popular generative AI applications since the technology's initial explosion in popularity. However, a Microsoft patent filing from late last month, recently uncovered by Patentlyze, aims to enhance how AI can edit real-time streaming.
The first claim describes an AI that listens for certain words in a broadcast's audio track and replaces them with new words based on information from the viewer's profile, such as age, location, and native language. Microsoft claims the AI would remove pauses and filler words to clean up the presentation, but it could also censor profanity and replace words based on internet searches.
Although the claim could also support instant fact-checking, it doesn't say whether it would tell users which edits were made or why. Furthermore, its ability to hide edits by adjusting lip movements in the intervening frames suggests viewers could end up watching AI-edited streams without realizing it. Real-time AI face swapping is already popular with scammers, so the ability to alter what is being said in a livestream could take misinformation and fraud to new levels.
Meanwhile, a separate, independent claim describes using the technology for translation. YouTube already supports AI audio translation, but Microsoft's patent would translate livestreams with matching lip sync. Moreover, unlike the first claim, the translator retains the original recording as a "ground truth."
These patents share a basic idea with others that involve changing the user experience in real time with AI. For example, an ambitious claim Microsoft filed in July aims to rewrite a game's code to add content based on player behavior.
Meanwhile, Sony recently filed multiple patents that would enhance game performance and reduce input latency by using AI to predict upcoming frames and which button a user will press next. Another would use AI to control game time progression, difficulty, and other aspects, or even fill in for players when they temporarily leave online sessions.

articles.title: EA producer found 20,000 archival media assets in secret physical vault at its HQ — Betacam, VHS, and D1 tapes among 6000 assets digitized to remaster seven classic games
articles.text:
EA producer found 20,000 archival media assets in secret physical vault at its HQ — Betacam, VHS, and D1 tapes among 6000 assets digitized to remaster seven classic games
This game preservation journey started with an accidental find.
Jim Vessella, a Senior Producer at the EA Partner teams at Electronic Arts, stumbled upon EA’s secret physical media vault at the company’s Redwood Shores campus. This wasn't just any storage room containing copies of old games; instead, it held nearly 20,000 archival media assets stored in various media, including Betacam, VHS, D1, Film Reels, CD-ROMs, and more. Vessella discovered it in 2022 and spent the next six months outside of his working hours unpacking the room. He was eventually joined by Greg Roensch, who worked with the EA Story initiative, which is the company’s own preservation project, and reorganized the room chronologically. From there, EA shared how this effort turned from an archival project into a remaster of several classic titles.
Vessella, who also worked on the Command & Conquer Remastered Collection in 2019, built a proposal to digitize the room once it was organized, with efforts starting in 2024. Two years later, the team working on the project had digitized 6,000 media assets and 2,500 hours of historical footage, including the Master Source tapes for the Wing Commander and Road Rash franchises. This has allowed the team to build Wing Commander III: Heart of the Tiger: 30th Anniversary Edition using those original master tapes. But more than just putting in new footage in the game, Vessella reached out to the Wing Commander community to help make the game playable on modern systems. This included Matt Wells (Mash), who built an Enhancement Patch for the Kilrathi Saga version of the game released in 1996, Owen “ODVS” Davies, who advised the EA team on full-motion video (FMV) restoration for some damaged tapes, and Ben “LOAF” Lesnick, who tweaked the game to fix the infamous insta-kill missile spam in Wing Commander IV.
EA also released Privateer 2: The Darkening: 30th Anniversary Edition with the help of Steve Hilliker, the original Cinematics Director of the game. It was actually a community member who said that they saw a video of Hilliker saying that he still has some of the master footage for the game stored on Digi 8. The team then reached out to the director, who found the entire collection in his attic. The team then commissioned Hilliker to digitize the tapes and create a “Director’s Cut” of the game’s cinematics. Matt once again stepped in and created an Enhancement Patch for Privateer 2, delivering a lot of quality-of-life improvements to the original game.
There was also a ton of work done on the original Wing Commander and the Wing Commander II sequel, plus the Road Rash retro titles. While purists might decry the “improvements” made to these titles that allowed them to be played on modern systems, the combined efforts of Electronic Arts, its passionate employees, GOG, and the community at large have allowed these games to be brought back to life. You could now get the entire Wing Commander collection and Road Rash: 30th Anniversary Edition on Steam, allowing you to reminisce about your favorite titles from the ‘90s and even allow your kids to see what gaming was like 30 years ago.
The recent release of these retro titles and the effort behind preserving them is a refreshing move after Sony announced that it will ditch physical games by 2028. While online game libraries like Steam are often more convenient for gamers, it has also raised the issue of ownership, with GOG taking a jab at Steam after the latter added a banner clarifying that you don’t own the games you buy on the platform. Despite Sony’s move away from physical media, other game companies have iterated their support for it. Nintendo says that fans like physical games, while Microsoft introduced the Xbox Disc to Digital feature that gave gamers the best of both worlds. GOG is even considering reviving physical game releases, although it admits that it still has to figure things out before it can start printing out physical game media.

Jowi Morales is a tech enthusiast with years of experience working in the industry. He’s been writing with several tech publications since 2021, where he’s been interested in tech hardware and consumer electronics.

articles.title: Le manga Zelda Ocarina of Time Perfect Edition prend des libertés avec le jeu, et ça vaut le détour
articles.text:
Vingt-huit ans après la Nintendo 64, Hyrule rouvre ses portes sur Switch 2. Le remake de The Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time est sorti le 5 novembre 2026, et notre test lui accorde toujours un 10 sur 10. Mais, une fois la console éteinte, l’histoire de Link peut aussi se lire.
Le manga Zelda Ocarina of Time d’Akira Himekawa, publié chez Soleil dans une Perfect Edition qui réunit toute l’adaptation en un seul livre, est disponible chez plusieurs e-commerçant :
C’est quoi, ce manga Zelda Ocarina of Time ?
Akira Himekawa est le pseudonyme d’un duo de deux autrices. Pour l’éditeur japonais Shōgakukan, elles ont adapté plusieurs épisodes de la saga en manga, d’Oracle of Seasons à Four Swords. Ocarina of Time est sans doute le plus connu. En France, Soleil l’avait d’abord publié en deux tomes en 2009.
The Legend of Zelda – Ocarina of Time – Perfect Edition
Auteur : Akira Himekawa
Éditeur : Soleil
Date de parution : 4/12/2024
Nombre de pages : 378 pages
Format : Grand format relié
Prix : 19,99 €
La Perfect Edition rassemble ces deux tomes, qui suivent chacun une époque de l’aventure : d’abord Link enfant, puis Link adulte. L’ensemble compte 378 pages, avec une couverture cartonnée, une jaquette et des premières pages en couleurs. Deux histoires bonus complètent le volume. La première raconte une fête chez les Kokiris centrée sur Skull Kid. La seconde suit un enfant Watarara, un peuple d’hommes-oiseaux créé spécialement pour le manga.
Le dessin respecte le design du jeu, si bien que l’on reconnaît sans peine les personnages et les décors. Le manga prend tout de même quelques libertés avec le scénario. Les connaisseurs remarqueront des différences avec le déroulé du jeu.
Le moment est dans tout les cas bien choisi. Le remake vient de sortir et remet l’histoire de Link en lumière. Le manga en donne une autre lecture, avec quelques scènes inventées pour l’occasion. Si vous accrochez, Soleil a publié d’autres Perfect Editions dans la même collection, dont Majora’s Mask à 19,99 €.

articles.title: Digitalgipfel 2026: Deutschland soll an die KI-Weltspitze – scheitert aber am Wesentlichen
articles.text:
Digitalgipfel 2026: Deutschland soll an die KI-Weltspitze – scheitert aber am Wesentlichen
Für Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) begann die Woche mit reichlich Aufbruchstimmung: Mit breitem Lächeln und sichtlich stolz schüttelte er am Montag das filigrane Händchen des deutschen Neura-Roboters in den Wilhelm Hallen in Berlin-Reinickendorf. Hier begann der große Digitalgipfel der Bundesregierung. Die Ansprache des Kanzlers: gewohnt selbstbewusst.
Deutschland bewege sich mit großem Erfolg bei der flächendeckenden Nutzung der Künstlichen Intelligenz, wolle technologische Abhängigkeiten weiter reduzieren und souverän werden. „Wir zeigen, Deutschland geht voran mit modernsten Technologien“, betont Merz. „Wir haben den Anspruch an uns selbst, führendes KI-Land auf der Welt zu werden. Und in die Richtung bewegen wir uns mit großem Erfolg.“
Da war doch was…
Platz eins in der Welt bei der Entwicklung und Nutzung Künstlicher Intelligenz? Großer Erfolg auf dem Weg dorthin? Blicken wir ein Jahr zurück: Bereits im November 2025 kündigte die Bundesregierung beim deutsch-französischen Gipfel zur europäischen digitalen Souveränität eine massive KI-Offensive, die Förderung und den Ausbau neuer Technologien und sogar eine konkrete deutsch-französische Kooperation an.
Die Abhängigkeit von außereuropäischen Infrastrukturen und den US-amerikanischen Big-Tech-Konzernen sollte deutlich reduziert und Europa auch mit Blick nach Fernost endlich konkurrenzfähig gemacht werden. Kritische Daten aller EU-Staaten sollten durch eigene Infrastruktur geschützt sein.
Mit dem französischen KI-Flaggschiff Mistral wurde eine umfangreiche Zusammenarbeit angekündigt. Kurswechsel war das Stichwort – weg vom Kundenstatus, hin zum Entwickler und Produzenten. Ein technologischer Selbstversorger wollte man sein, der seine Potenziale erkennt und umsetzt. Global bestens vernetzt, dennoch eigenständig und sicher – es klang so schön.
Deutschland bleibt Kunde
Ein Jahr später sieht die Realität leider erwartbar anders aus. Die Mistral-Partnerschaft wurde auf Eis gelegt und plötzlich deutlich diffuser beschrieben, zu einem Rahmenvertrag, auch mit dem Softwarekonzern SAP, kam es nie. Die damit verbundene Vision der eigenen KI-Verwaltungssoftware sowie -Agenten wurde vorerst herunterpriorisiert. An der Zusammenarbeit wolle man, so stellte das Digitalministerium klar, aber grundsätzlich festhalten. Allerdings deutlich zurückhaltender als noch im Vorjahr.
Umtriebig war man dennoch und neue Kooperationen wurden stattdessen geschlossen – nach einer, nennen wir es mal, deutlich universelleren Strategie: Die Nachrichtendienste BND und MAD sowie der Verfassungsschutz sollen künftig auf die Google-Cloud-Plattform setzen.
Nvidia wird offensiv umworben und mit strategischen Absichtserklärungen ausgestattet und die bayerische Landesregierung sorgte zwischenzeitlich mit der Ankündigung eines Milliardenpaketes für die Verwaltungssoftware von US-Hyperscaler Microsoft für Furore.
Immerhin wurde dieses Vorhaben nach internem Disput und großem öffentlichen Protest wieder gekippt. Dennoch bescheinigen Experten und vor allem Datenschützer Deutschland insgesamt hier keine sichere Zukunft, erst recht keine souveräne.
XXL-Plan für vier Jahre
Nun soll Deutschland also im Rahmen eines 18-Punkte-Maßnahmenpaketes bis 2030 seine allgemeine Rechenkapazität verdoppeln und seine KI-Kapazitäten sogar idealerweise vervierfachen. Startups und Forschungseinrichtungen sollen weiter gefördert, die Wirtschaft mit umfangreichen Ressourcen für die Entwicklung von industrieller KI ausgestattet werden. Im Rahmen der Hightech-Agenda sollen zusätzlich ganz neue Ansätze wie Weltmodelle und physische KI weiter erforscht werden.
Die Vorhaben sind zahlreich und gewohnt spektakulär. Auch einzelne Bundesländer gehen mit einem Rahmenvertrag für eine souveräne Open-Source-Bildungsplattform neue Wege. Den gesamten Maßnahmenkatalog soll jeder bei der Bundesregierung selbst nachlesen können, denn er würde hier den Rahmen sprengen.
Nur so viel: Einen verbindlichen Zeitplan für den Großteil der Maßnahmen, etwa auch für einzelne Behörden, gibt es nicht. Wieder nicht! Einen Aktionsplan soll es für die Verwaltung geben. Verbindlichkeit und Tempo lesen sich hier nicht heraus. Und vier Jahre globale KI-Entwicklung vergehen im Flug.
Das ewige Dilemma
Zugegeben, die Herausforderung, eigene Technologien zu entwickeln, dabei jedoch gleichzeitig permanent wirtschaftlich wettbewerbsfähig zu bleiben, ist gewaltig. Das braucht durchaus Zeit und Flexibilität.
Bereits im t3n-Interview Anfang des Jahres unterstrich Digitalminister Karsten Wildberger (CDU), die Strategie, langfristig digitale Souveränität aufzubauen, jedoch in Handelsbeziehung und Partnerschaft zu Partnern außerhalb Europas.
Dieser Weg ist vertretbar. Allein unsere Chip- und Rohstoffabhängigkeit bietet keine machbaren Alternativen. Ein rein europäischer Weg wirkt dementsprechend naiv. Auch der Anspruch an Aufbruchstimmung und Tempo, etwa beim Bau von Rechenzentren, ist zwingend notwendig. Ein starkes Selbstbewusstsein mit exzellenten deutschen Forschungseinrichtungen ist absolut legitim. Aber…
Macht endlich Tempo!
Zentral ist jedoch hier der Faktor Zeit. Die Bilanz zwischen den beiden Gipfeln macht derzeit wenig Hoffnung. Nun stehen also gerade einmal vier Jahre auf der neuen X‑Achse. Auch wenn Überregulierung hierbei nicht das Ziel sein darf, muss bei den wesentlichen Stellschrauben globaler Kooperation in Zukunft besser hingeschaut werden. Nicht umsonst haben die USA schon vor langer Zeit mit dem Cloud Act zu große Ausrufezeichen in eigener Sache gesetzt.
Wenig Zeit bis 2030, die hoffentlich entschlossen und konkret genutzt wird. Ansonsten bleibt Deutschland weiterhin Kunde und das Warenregal größtenteils „Made in America“.
Traumtänzerei….der Zug ist für Deutschland schon lange abgefahren….für alles.

articles.title: Que el cuero más antiguo del mundo tenga 7.200 años no es sorpresa. Que esté en Granada, sí
articles.text:
Hace aproximadamente 7.200 años, alguien curtió una piel de cabra y le hizo cuatro agujeros. No se sabe bien cómo, pero acabó en la cueva prehistórica de los Murciélagos, en el municipio granadino de Albuñol, un lugar que durante milenios sirvió como cementerio. Ese fragmento de cuero probablemente formó parte de un ajuar funerario, quizás como envoltorio del cuerpo o como prenda.
En el siglo XIX, unos mineros que buscaban galena lo emparedaron, no se sabe si porque no sabían que estaba o les dio igual, pero ahí quedó incrustado entre las piedras. Hasta que lo encontraron y le pusieron fecha.
El hallazgo. Un equipo internacional, con la University College Dublin y la Universidad de Alcalá al frente, ha datado con radiocarbono la pieza, que conserva el pelo en una cara y huellas de curtido en la otra. El resultado es una edad de entre 7.246 y 7.008 años calibrados antes del presente (tomando 1950 como referencia). El estudio considera que los dos fragmentos hallados son probablemente del mismo animal. También han recuperado fragmentos de ADN humano que encajan con la posibilidad de que alguien manipulara la pieza o simplemente se la pusiera, así como de un cánido, probablemente posterior.
Por qué importa. Porque según el equipo, es la primera vez que se obtiene ADN nuclear de cabras domésticas de la península ibérica. Además, es uno de los genomas más antiguos logrados a partir de restos orgánicos fuera de zonas de mucho frío o de alta montaña. Hasta ahora lo habíamos visto en contextos de hielo, como el cuero del Hombre de los Hielos o unas polainas de piel de cabra de los Alpes, pero es raro que un ADN tan antiguo aguante en una zona cálida.
Una cueva única en lo arqueológico y en lo ambiental. La Cueva de los Murciélagos de Albuñol está a unos siete kilómetros del mar Mediterráneo y a 450 metros de altitud. Según el equipo, sus condiciones microambientales han permitido que se conserven, por desecación, materiales orgánicos que casi nunca sobreviven como estos fragmentos de cuero. Y es un auténtico filón para la arqueología: allí se ha encontrado la cestería más antigua del sur de Europa y la primera evidencia de arquería del Neolítico antiguo, con cuerdas de arco de hace unos 7.000 años.
Como mencionábamos en la intro, esta cueva se ha usado largo y tendido como cementerio: según el paper, este uso ha tenido cinco fases. Empieza hace unos 9.500 años, en el Mesolítico, sigue en el Neolítico antiguo, medio y final, y acaba en la Edad del Bronce, hace unos 3.900-3.700 años.
De las primeras cabras domésticas. La genética la identifica como una hembra de cabra doméstica (Capra hircus), pero es que cabras se domesticaron en el Creciente Fértil y la prueba más antigua de su uso doméstico en el sur de la península ibérica data de hace 7.500 años de la mano de los primeros agricultores y pastores, según este estudio sobre la colonización marítima del Mediterráneo occidental por los primeros agricultores.
La cabra de Albuñol no tenía ascendencia africana, lo que apunta a que esa mezcla llegaría después. Entre las razas comparadas, la más afín es la bermeya, pero solo se incluyeron cuatro razas españolas y además, la muestra es escasa.

articles.title: Un ciberataque contra neveras y congeladores de cientos de supermercados de Francia provoca pérdidas millonarias
articles.text:
Un ciberataque no siempre termina con el robo de contraseñas o con los ordenadores de una empresa bloqueados. En Francia, por ejemplo, cientos de supermercados descubrieron que sus neveras y congeladores habían dejado de funcionar después de que unos atacantes manipularan sus sistemas de refrigeración a distancia. Por desgracia, algunas instalaciones llegaron a alcanzar los 50 grados durante varias horas y se vieron obligados a retirar grandes cantidades de alimentos con posibles pérdidas económicas de millones de euros.
Según informó Reuters, el incidente ocurrió durante la noche del 11 al 12 de octubre y afectó a establecimientos de cadenas como Intermarché, Carrefour, Monoprix y Coopérative U. Los atacantes consiguieron modificar los parámetros de funcionamiento de los equipos aprovechando el sistema que permite gestionar su temperatura de forma remota, y esto provocó que en algunos establecimientos también se registraran pequeños incendios.
Los fallos de seguridad ya habían puesto en alerta a los investigadores
Buena parte de los equipos afectados utilizaban tecnología de la compañía danesa Danfoss, y esta reconoció que algunos funcionaban con programas antiguos o versiones que no estaban actualizadas. El problema es que ya se conocía el error, dado que los investigadores de Claroty habían identificado vulnerabilidades en determinados controladores de refrigeración meses antes.
Su investigación mostró que podías acceder desde internet a miles de dispositivos de este tipo, pero todavía no se ha confirmado qué fallo concreto permitió ejecutar el ataque. Así, la Fiscalía de París abrió una investigación para identificar a los responsables y las cadenas afectadas, por su parte, trabajan en recuperar sus instalaciones.
Por desgracia, el incidente no es un caso aislado. A principios de noviembre, se registraron nuevos ataques contra sistemas de refrigeración en otros países europeos y sigue sin demostrarse una autoría común. Todo lo ocurrido deja una preocupación que va más allá de los supermercados franceses, ya que cualquier instalación conectada a Internet puede convertirse en el objetivo de un hacker si sus sistemas de control no están protegidos correctamente.
