articles.title: Llega la primera movilización europea contra los centros de datos: “No queremos ser el patio trasero de nadie”
articles.text:
Llega la primera movilización europea contra los centros de datos: “No queremos ser el patio trasero de nadie”
España es uno de los 15 países en los que hay convocados este sábado diversos actos para exigir una moratoria en la construcción de estas infraestructuras
Este sábado hay convocadas movilizaciones en 15 países europeos para solicitar una moratoria en la construcción de centros de datos, esas instalaciones repletas de servidores y procesadores sin los que no funcionaría internet y que han florecido en los últimos años de la mano de la irrupción comercial de la inteligencia artificial (IA). España aglutina 22 de las 90 acciones de protesta previstas, que se desarrollarán en ciudades como Barcelona, Madrid, Sevilla y Pamplona. Es la primera iniciativa de este tipo coordinada a escala europea.
“Pedimos una moratoria inmediata sobre la construcción de nuevos centros de datos a gran escala a nivel local, nacional y europeo”, resume Aurora Gómez, de 43 años y nacida en Ballesteros de Calatrava, Ciudad Real. Esta psicóloga es la fundadora del colectivo Tu Nube Seca Mi Río y coordinadora de los eventos organizados en España. “Los gobiernos, la UE y las grandes empresas tecnológicas están avanzando a toda velocidad con la construcción de estas instalaciones. Exigimos que se detenga de inmediato este proceso, que se lleve a cabo un análisis exhaustivo de las repercusiones medioambientales, democráticas y sociales, y que se establezcan marcos claros para decidir si deben construirse centros de datos a gran escala y en qué condiciones”, apunta.
Países como Irlanda, Países Bajos o Singapur ya han puesto en marcha moratorias de este tipo. En EE UU, que concentra la mitad de los centros de datos del mundo, la carta blanca otorgada a la industria por el presidente Trump ha provocado la reacción de los votantes en las elecciones de medio mandato. Los analistas creen que el deseo de imponer una moratoria y ordenar el crecimiento del sector explica parte del impulso que ha permitido al Partido Demócrata arrollar en los comicios, asegurándose el control del Senado y la Cámara de Representantes, aunque también hay republicanos que comparten esa inquietud.
La resistencia ante estas infraestructuras es poliédrica. Sus externalidades negativas son variadas: consumen mucha energía, hasta el punto de subir la factura de la luz en algunas regiones; generan poco empleo, más allá del necesario para construirlos; necesitan agua, hacen un ruido constante, acaparan y modifican mucho territorio y se sabe también que pueden generar problemas para la salud de los vecinos.
Gómez no quiere ver todo eso en España. “En Irlanda, los centros de datos suponen ya más del 30% de la demanda estatal de electricidad, según la operadora Eirgrid. En Latinoamérica han exacerbado sequías. No queremos ser el patio trasero de nadie, queremos juntarnos en las plazas públicas y defender nuestra agua, clima y territorios”, sentencia. La vertiente internacional del movimiento es, en su opinión, esencial para su crecimiento. Alemania, Austria, Bélgica, Dinamarca, Finlandia, Francia, Irlanda, Italia, Países Bajos, Polonia y Reino Unido participan también en la movilización.
“Llevamos un año pensando en esta campaña, y entendiendo que las movilizaciones de estos días son solo un punto de partida. Cada país tiene unas características diversas, desde el tiempo que llevan implantados los centros de datos hasta la situación política, el estado de sus resistencias o los impactos que más preocupan. Hemos buscado una coordinación plural, donde desde la parte europea se aporten la idea central de moratoria y las comunidades puedan adaptar las demandas específicas y los formatos de acción que mejor encajen”, explica.
En España hay convocadas para este sábado 22 movilizaciones de naturaleza muy diversa. “Por ejemplo, habrá manifestaciones más clásicas en Zaragoza, y paseos reivindicativos en Madrid. Pero también bicicletadas alrededor de los centros de datos, medir la distancia del centro de datos a su vivienda, grupos que se juntan a hacer peticiones públicas de transparencia, recitales de poesía o lecturas de fanzines. Cada comunidad elige la manera de protestar que mejor le encaje, que a la vez sirva de punto de encuentro y debate”, señala Gómez.
Aunque en países como EE UU el debate en torno a los centros de datos ha entrado de lleno en la conversación pública o incluso en la campaña electoral, en España todavía no estamos en ese momento. Con todo, Gómez detecta un creciente interés en el asunto, acaso alimentado por la animadversión que despiertan los dueños de las grandes tecnológicas. “En los cuatro años que Tu Nube Seca Mi Río lleva como colectivo hemos visto una sensibilidad creciente respecto a los impactos de los centros de datos y una mayor preocupación de los europeos respecto a este tema, como refleja una encuesta que hicimos hace un año”, indica. “La gente en lo rural se está levantando contra los centros de datos, y en las ciudades cada vez están más preocupados por los impactos de la IA. Ambas son dos caras de la misma moneda, y es ese hermanamiento entre las luchas rurales y de ciudad lo que puede dar todo el impulso que necesitamos para parar un problema tan grande”.

articles.title: Religiöse Gründe: Uni-Mitarbeiter verweigert KI-Einsatz
articles.text:
Religiöse Ausnahmegenehmigung: Dieser Mann muss im Büro offiziell keine KI mehr nutzen
Der Einsatz von KI erhitzt seit Längerem die Gemüter. Die einen sorgen sich um Cybergefahren oder kritisieren den KI-bedingten Stellenabbau. Andere fragen sich, welche Auswirkungen die neue Technologie konkret auf das menschliche Denken hat. Zu ihnen gehört David Durman. Er arbeitet als Verwaltungsmitarbeiter an der University of Kentucky und bezeichnet sich selbst als Humanist. Wie Religion News berichtet, hat er jetzt eine religiös begründete Ausnahmegenehmigung erhalten, die ihn vom KI-Einsatz befreit.
KI nicht mit Humanismus vereinbar?
Immer mehr Menschen müssen sich am Arbeitsplatz mit neuen KI-Tools auseinandersetzen. Oft sollen sie Prozesse beschleunigen und so die Produktivität steigern. Als die University of Kentucky ihre Mitarbeiter:innen aufforderte, KI in ihre Arbeitsabläufe zu integrieren, machte sich Durman Sorgen. Er hatte das Gefühl, er solle sein Denken in der täglichen Arbeit an einen Chatbot auslagern. Das empfand er als Verstoß gegen seine Überzeugungen.
„Der Prozess und die Arbeit, die damit verbunden sind, Situationen zu durchdenken – im Rahmen meiner Arbeit, meiner Ethik und der Art und Weise, wie ich mit anderen Menschen umgehe – sind ein wesentlicher Bestandteil meiner Entwicklung zu einem moralischen Menschen“, erklärte er im Interview mit Religion News. „Und diese Arbeit auszulagern, unabhängig davon, ob sie anstrengend ist oder nicht, untergräbt meine Fähigkeit, moralisch zu handeln.“
Mithilfe der American Humanist Association beantragte er eine Ausnahmeregelung gemäß eines Bundesgesetzes, das es Beschäftigten erlaubt, Änderungen ihrer Arbeitsanforderungen zu beantragen, um ihren religiösen Überzeugungen gerecht zu werden. Im September stimmte die Universität zu: Durman muss jetzt keine KI mehr für seine Arbeit einsetzen. Vertreter:innen der American Humanist Association gehen davon aus, dass Durman der erste Humanist ist, der eine solche KI-Ausnahmeregelung erzielen konnte.
Wie KI das kritische Denken untergräbt
Durman ist nicht der Einzige, dem es widerstrebt, sein Denken an eine KI auszulagern. Zuletzt forderten zahlreiche Mathematiker:innen in der neugegründeten Association for Human Mathematics, die Disziplin solle in menschlicher Hand bleiben. Kurz zuvor hatte OpenAI auf einen Schlag 722 Fachartikel veröffentlicht. Sie beweisen oder widerlegen mathematische Probleme, an denen Wissenschaftler:innen bisher gescheitert waren. Der Verband argumentiert, mathematischer Fortschritt erfordere menschliches Fachwissen, das durch sorgfältiges Denken entstehe. Die automatisierte Produktion und Rezeption von Mathematik untergrabe daher die intellektuellen Grundlagen des Fachgebiets.
Die Sorge, KI könne das Urteilsvermögen beeinträchtigen, ist nicht unbegründet. Laut einer Studie von Microsoft und der Carnegie Mellon University könnten Menschen, die sich zu sehr auf KI verlassen, die Fähigkeit verlieren, kritisch zu denken. Die Forscher:innen befragten 319 Personen, die beruflich Daten oder Informationen auswerten, zu ihren KI-Gewohnheiten. Sie beobachteten: Je stärker die Nutzer:innen von den Fähigkeiten der KI überzeugt waren, desto eigenständiger ließen sie die KI arbeiten. Dadurch könne eine übermäßige Abhängigkeit von KI-Tools ohne nachträgliche Prüfung entstehen.
Auch Papst Leo XIV. äußert sich kritisch
Durman geht sogar noch einen Schritt weiter. Er befürchtet, dass KI die Gesellschaft auf schädliche Weise beeinflussen könnte. Als Humanist glaube er an die Bedeutung der menschlichen Entfaltung: „Auf gesellschaftlicher Ebene denke ich, dass der Einsatz von KI-Technologie dem zuwiderläuft.“ Auch Papst Leo XIV. hatte sich zuvor ähnlich geäußert. In seiner Enzyklika warnte er Anfang dieses Jahres, dass KI die Demokratie und die Menschenwürde schwächen könnte. Bei Missbrauch könnten KI-Tools einer kleinen Elite zudem zusätzliche Macht verleihen, während der Rest der Menschheit zurückbleibe.

articles.title: Prendre un bain de pieds en roulant ? L'incroyable brevet déposé par cette marque chinoise
articles.text:
Innover pour vendre toujours plus, tel est le mantra des constructeurs chinois, même quand les inventions n’ont pas grand sens. Pour attirer le monde, la marque Deepal vient ainsi de déposer un brevet pour un bain de pieds intégré à l’habitacle de ses véhicules. Aussi farfelue soit-elle, l’idée est pourtant bien réelle avec plusieurs dispositifs permettant effectivement de se relaxer en se faisant conduire. Reste à voir si la chose passera le cap de la série.
Pour assurer une sécurité maximale en utilisation, le système intègre un mécanisme rétractable reliant directement le bac à eau au siège passager avant. Lorsqu’il n’est pas utilisé, l’ensemble est plié sous le siège, ce qui limite son encombrement. Et que se passera-t-il lorsque le véhicule roulera sur des bosses et abordera des courbes à toute allure ? Vous n’en mettrez pas de partout, rassurez-vous.
Virages et bosses : comment éviter l’inondation dans l’habitacle ?
L’ensemble retient en effet des dispositifs anti éclaboussures, des orifices pour l’écoulement de l’eau ainsi que des bras contrant le balancement. Le bac est en ce sens parfaitement stable en toutes circonstances et se voit relié à un mini réseau de canalisation intégré au véhicule. Un système de désinfection est également de la partie pour assurer une hygiène optimale utilisation après utilisation. Oui, c’est tout de même assez complexe.
Et honnêtement, on cherche encore l’utilité de la chose. Les responsables de Deepal, eux, assurent que cet accessoire « vise à résoudre les problèmes liés à l’intégration d’équipements de soins des pieds dans les véhicules, notamment en ce qui concerne l’espace intérieur occupé et la difficulté d’adapter ces dispositifs aux structures existantes ». On reste bien dubitatifs. Peut-être que les bains de pieds sont populaires en Chine ?
Quel futur modèle pourrait accueillir cette option inédite ?
Ce n’est en tout cas pas la première fois qu’une auto est capable de prendre soin de vos pieds. Audi avait jadis proposé sur l’A8 une option proposant de masser vos pieds en les plaquant au dos du siège passager avant. Mais il n’était alors pas question de bain chaud… Deepal passe donc une étape supérieure pour assurer le confort et la détente de ses occupants. Quel modèle pourrait effectivement adopter la chose si elle se concrétise ?
Le SUV S09 serait un bon candidat puisqu’il s’agit du fer de lance de la marque chinoise. Avec ses 5,21 mètres de long et ses six places, l’engin pourra accommoder sans problème un tel équipement. Mais cela devrait néanmoins coûter cher, et chauffer l’eau ne sera pas non plus gratuit. Fort heureusement, le S09 est un modèle à prolongateur d’autonomie, ce qui signifie que son rayon d’action ne devrait pas trop être impacté.

articles.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
articles.text:
Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down.
Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.
That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.
The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development.
But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development.
Here are some of the biggest takeaways.
AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development
One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress.
Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5.
For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.”
Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps
Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models.
Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote.
Anthropic is keeping key information secret
Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions.
And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X.
METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.”
METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said.
In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not.
“We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.”
McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety.
Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected
The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability.
For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028.
The report provides evidence about just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development.
Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering.
On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.”
Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety
Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month.
Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.”
Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post.
The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.”
Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs
Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities. METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.”
For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence. While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development.
Others have called for more direct action. In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility.
And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify. Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

articles.title: Clap de fin pour le Tesla Cybertruck : chronique d’un échec industriel annoncé
articles.text:
Il devait redéfinir le marché automobile américain et faire passer les Ford F-150 pour des reliques du passé. Le Tesla Cybertruck restera finalement dans les livres d’histoire comme l’un des plus spectaculaires dérapages industriels modernes.
Elon Musk a annoncé, le 6 novembre 2026, sur X (ex-Twitter) la fin de production du pick-up à la Gigafactory d’Austin vers la mi-2027. Tesla veut utiliser l’espace libéré pour produire davantage de Cybercab, son robotaxi sans volant ni pédales, fabriqué également à Austin et qui a commencé à transporter des clients payants dans la ville depuis septembre.
Du mirage à moins de 40 000 dollars au gouffre à six chiffres
Dévoilé en grande pompe fin 2019, le Cybertruck est resté dans les mémoires pour les couacs de sa présentation (vitres brisées et grandes promesses). Tesla annonçait alors une version de base à 39 900 dollars (environ 35 800 €), un tarif dont le pick-up ne s’est jamais approché.
Après de nombreux retards dans son développement et son industrialisation, la facture a rapidement dérapé : les premiers clients de la série Foundation ont dû débourser plus de 100 000 dollars (environ 89 700 €). L’autonomie a fondu, elle aussi. Tesla promettait jusqu’à 500 miles (environ 800 km), alors que la version Premium vendue aujourd’hui affiche 325 miles (environ 523 km) selon le cycle américain EPA.
Surtout, l’équation économique était viciée dès l’origine. En s’entêtant à concevoir une carrosserie en tôle d’acier inoxydable laminée à froid, Tesla s’est enfermé dans des coûts fixes bien trop élevés qui n’avaient de sens qu’avec des volumes de production importants. Tesla avait prévu la ligne du Cybertruck au Texas pour 250 000 exemplaires par an.
Or, les réservations à 100 dollars, remboursables, ne se sont jamais traduites en commandes réelles. Elon Musk en revendiquait plus d’un million en octobre 2023, et des estimations indépendantes en comptaient près de deux millions.
Il restera le plus gros flop de Tesla
Tesla ne publie pas ses ventes modèle par modèle, mais Kelley Blue Book estime à environ 70 000 les Cybertruck vendus aux États-Unis depuis 2024. La demande s’est tarie dès que le premier cercle des inconditionnels de la marque et des influenceurs a été servi. Coincé par son poids et ses arêtes coupantes, le Cybertruck n’a jamais pu être homologué en Europe ni sur les grands marchés mondiaux, réduisant son terrain de jeu à la seule Amérique du Nord, où les professionnels et les utilisateurs de pick-up traditionnels l’ont largement délaissé, notamment en raison de ses limites à l’usage.
Sur les neuf premiers mois de 2026, Cox Automotive estime à 11 586 le nombre de Cybertruck vendus aux États-Unis, dont 4 323 au troisième trimestre. À ce rythme, Tesla en écoule environ 15 000 par an, soit seize fois moins que ce que la ligne d’Austin devait produire.
Pour achever le spectacle avec un joli coup de cynisme commercial, Tesla avait, la veille de l’annonce, gelé les commandes de la version d’accès Dual Motor et relevé les prix des versions restantes. La Premium AWD, désormais la moins chère, passe de 84 990 à 92 490 dollars (environ 83 000 €), soit 8,8 % de plus, et le Cyberbeast grimpe à 102 490 dollars (environ 91 900 €). C’est la deuxième hausse en moins de trois mois, après celle d’août. Une technique classique pour presser le citron des derniers acheteurs, avant de tirer le rideau.
Pour les propriétaires, Elon Musk s’est voulu rassurant en répondant à un internaute sur X : la flotte de Cybertruck « sera là pour longtemps ». Il n’a en revanche rien précisé sur la durée de vente des stocks, ni sur les pièces détachées et l’entretien, un point sensible pour un véhicule aux panneaux de carrosserie uniques.
En voulant imposer un délire de science-fiction plutôt qu’un outil de travail rationnel, Tesla a gaspillé des milliards de dollars et des années d’ingénierie qui auraient été infiniment plus utiles pour renouveler les Model 3 et Model Y ou lancer une compacte populaire à 25 000 euros. Ses avancées techniques (l’architecture électrique en 48 volts, la direction sans liaison mécanique dite steer-by-wire) serviront aux futurs modèles. Wes Morrill, l’ingénieur en chef du projet, assure d’ailleurs que le Cybertruck « survit à travers le Cybercab ». Commercialement, en revanche, le mastodonte en inox restera un caprice d’ingénieur devenu trop lourd à porter.

articles.title: Un an après le record historique du Bitcoin, la crypto va-t-elle bientôt repartir ?
articles.text:
Souvenez-vous, le 6 octobre 2025, le Bitcoin a passé la barre des 126 000 dollars pour la première fois de son histoire. Derrière ce record, on trouvait notamment les fonds indiciels (ETF) consacrés au Bitcoin, lancés aux États-Unis 21 mois plus tôt, qui attiraient des milliards de dollars de capitaux. Grâce à eux, les investisseurs institutionnels, comme les fonds de pension et les gestionnaires d’actifs, se sont massivement exposés à la crypto. En parallèle, l’administration Trump multipliait les signaux favorables aux cryptomonnaies, signe que la guerre contre l’industrie crypto arrivait à son terme.
L’euphorie a été de courte durée, comme c’est souvent le cas avec les cryptomonnaies. Le 10 octobre 2025, quatre jours seulement après le record, l’annonce de nouveaux droits de douane américains contre la Chine a fait plonger les marchés financiers. La dégringolade a déclenché une cascade de liquidations. Plus de 19 milliards de dollars de positions ont été éliminées sur les marchés dérivés de cryptomonnaies. C’était le début d’une longue phase de baisse pour le roi Bitcoin.
Une année 2026 dans le rouge
Tout au long de l’année 2026, le Bitcoin n’a cessé de perdre de la valeur. Le premier trimestre a donné le ton, avec une baisse d’environ 19 % en trois mois. Le Bitcoin est ensuite repassé sous les 59 000 dollars, perdant plus de la moitié de sa valeur par rapport à son record. Le mois de juin s’est d’ailleurs imposé comme le pire mois de l’histoire du Bitcoin en 4 ans.
Les mauvaises nouvelles tirant le cours vers le bas se sont accumulées. Le conflit entre les États-Unis et l’Iran a fait flamber le prix du pétrole et relancé les craintes d’inflation, éloignant les investisseurs des actifs les plus risqués. Dans ce contexte, les ETF Bitcoin ont enchaîné les fuites de capitaux. Plus de 8 milliards de dollars se sont envolés. Cette année, la crypto a aussi subi la concurrence accrue de l’intelligence artificielle. Sous toutes les lèvres, l’IA générative accapare désormais une grande partie des investissements. En octobre, le piratage record de Binance, avec plus de 6 milliards de dollars dérobés, a de nouveau plombé le cours de la crypto. En ce début novembre, le Bitcoin évolue toujours très loin de son record historique.
C’est loin d’être la première fois que le Bitcoin joue les montagnes russes. Lors des précédents cycles, le Bitcoin avait baissé de 77 % à 85 % par rapport à ses sommets, sans que ça remette en question la valeur de la cryptomonnaie. Cette fois, la baisse est nettement moins brutale que lors des précédents cycles. Grâce aux investisseurs institutionnels, le marché crypto s’est considérablement stabilisé.
À lire aussi : « Mode bunker » – pourquoi l’IA sème la panique chez les investisseurs crypto
Le Bitcoin va-t-il repartir en 2027 ?
Pour certains analystes, le plus dur est d’ores et déjà passé. La banque Bernstein, connue pour son optimisme au sujet du Bitcoin, table sur un nouveau record, autour des 150 000 dollars, d’ici à la mi-2027. Selon la banque, le Bitcoin pourrait même grimper jusqu’à 200 000 dollars. La crypto profiterait des inquiétudes croissantes autour de la dette des États. La dette publique américaine avoisine en effet les 40 000 milliards de dollars, rappelle Bernstein. Et les taux d’intérêt auxquels les États empruntent ne cessent de grimper. Aux États-Unis, le taux à 10 ans dépasse les 5 %. En France, il a franchi ce seuil symbolique le 21 octobre, une première depuis 2002. Or, plus les taux montent, plus la charge de la dette s’alourdit.
Pour s’en sortir, les gouvernements pourraient être tentés de faire tourner la planche à billets, ce qui ferait théoriquement perdre de la valeur aux monnaies traditionnelles, comme le dollar ou l’euro. Dans ce scénario, les investisseurs se tourneraient alors progressivement vers des actifs dont l’offre ne dépend pas des banques centrales, comme l’or ou le Bitcoin. Le même argument est repris par Jonathan Herscovici, fondateur de la plateforme d’épargne en Bitcoin StackinSat. Selon lui, une crise de confiance dans les dettes publiques pourrait pousser les investisseurs vers des actifs rares, comme le Bitcoin, considérés comme des protections contre l’inflation des monnaies. C’est pourquoi il pense « que 2027 pourrait marquer un tournant majeur dans son adoption ».
D’autres observateurs du marché se montrent plus prudents. Citi et Standard Chartered ont tous revu à la baisse leurs objectifs de cours pour 2026. Pour Javier Molina, analyste chez eToro, tout dépendra du retour des acheteurs sur le marché des cryptomonnaies. Selon l’expert, « une reprise durable nécessitera une véritable demande à l’achat, et pas seulement des rachats de positions vendeuses ». Il estime que l’enjeu sera d’« attirer des flux entrants durables vers les ETF », les fonds à l’origine du précédent record du Bitcoin.
« Le bitcoin s’institutionnalise de plus en plus, mais reste vulnérable. Les ETF ont transformé l’accès au marché, même si la liquidité, les taux d’intérêt et le dollar continuent d’influencer ses performances », ajoute Javier Molina.
Par ailleurs, le halving, la prochaine mise à jour du protocole Bitcoin, n’est pas prévu avant 2028. Historiquement, c’est cet évènement qui signe le coup d’envoi d’un nouveau marché haussier. Si le scénario se répète, le prochain grand pic ne serait donc pas pour 2027, mais plutôt pour 2029. Les analystes de Bernstein visent d’ailleurs un Bitcoin à 300 000 dollars cette année-là.

articles.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
articles.text:
A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
Scientists have developed a promising new method that could read quantum information with 99.85% accuracy while barely disturbing the qubit itself.
- Date:

- Summary:
- Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient.
- Share:
One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.
Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.
The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.
Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult
Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.
This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.
"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.
To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.
The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.
Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.
"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.
A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal
The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.
Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.
These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.
"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.
The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.
The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.
Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.
"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.
How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information
To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.
One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.
The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.
According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.
"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.
This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.
A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage
Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.
Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."
The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.
"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.
This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.
That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.
Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor
The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.
Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.
Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.
The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.
Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.
"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."
The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.
Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance
In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.
This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.
The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.
"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.
The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.
This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.
Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy
To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.
These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.
The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.
According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.
The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.
However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.
Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?
Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.
The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.
What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.
"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.
This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.
The research offers two potentially significant advances.
From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.
From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.
If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.
More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.
